Every value in air is a form: an immutable, JSON-like tree of scalars and
containers. Code is a form too, which is why a rule can rewrite a program and a
program can build a rule. This chapter describes the form itself, quoted forms
(holds), mutables, and the three equality relations.

A form is an immutable object that contains actual data. Strings, symbols,
numbers (see 

Numbers for the eight numeric leaves),
booleans, and the null value naught are all considered subtypes of the
form type.

Collections: Sequences (whitespace-separated elements surrounded by
parentheses) and mappings (paired values with keys, e.g., (a=1 b=2 c=3))
are forms.

Hybrid Forms: Forms can include both sequential and mapping values: (f 1 2 a=3 b=4) is a form with three sequential elements and two mapping
elements. Keyword elements do not need to come in any particular order, and
their ordering is not preserved ((f 1 2 a=3 b=4), (a=3 b=4 f 1 2), and
(f a=3 1 b=4 2) are all equal forms).

Empty Form: There is exactly one empty form (), which is considered
logically false and identical to naught (acting as a nil value).

Querying: Collection contents can be queried by treating them as
functions; for a form f equal to (1 (2 3) a=(g h i)), (f 1) returns
1, (f 2) returns (2 3), and (f :a) returns (g h i). Extended
argument lists forward through the return value (e.g., (f 2 1) returns
2).

Updating: (with form k1 v1 …) replaces the subform at each key (a
sequence key is a nested path, and an integer key n + 1 appends);
(update coll key f) replaces it with (f old); (update-in coll k1 … kn f) does the same at a deep path, with a missing key yielding naught to
f; and (wout form k…) removes the subform. Extra arguments to f are
written with part, as in (update-in m :a (part + 10)).

The wildcard key: the lone : names every entry of a level — each
sequence element in order, then each map value in canonical key order (the
printer’s order; air does not preserve the order in which keys were written).
In get it selects the whole level and maps the rest of the path over each
entry, so the result is an ordinary sequence and map values lose their keys
((get ((a=1) (a=2)) : :a) is (1 2), (get (a=1 b=2) :) is (1 2), and
(get (1 2 a=3) :) is (1 2 3)); in with a scalar is broadcast to
every entry ((with (a=1 b=2) : 9) is (a=9 b=9)) and a container supplies
one value per entry in that same canonical order ((with (b=2 a=1) : (7 8))
is (a=7 b=8)), with each sequence position and map key kept in place; in
wout and drop it removes every entry, and as an intermediate step it
applies the rest of the path to each one ((wout ((a=1 x=0) (a=2 x=0)) : :x)
is ((a=1) (a=2))). A scalar is its own sole entry and naught is empty; a
table has its own path rules (: keeps its meaning of all rows or all
columns, and a lone : raises). When any wout key is :, its key
arguments form one path.

Map entries can be unintuitive. Map values are paired in canonical key
order, not source order, so (with (b=2 a=1) : (7 8)) is (a=7 b=8) —
write the values in the order the printer would show the keys. On a mixed
level the sequence elements always come first, so
(with (1 2 a=3) : (7 8 9)) is (7 8 a=9). A scalar sets every entry
((with (a=1 b=2) : 9) is (a=9 b=9)), but a one-element form is one value,
not a broadcast, so (with (a=1 b=2) : (9)) raises — air never collapses
(9) into 9. And get returns the values alone, so (get (a=1 b=2) :) is
(1 2), with no record of which key held which value.

Locating: (where coll obj depth=d) finds every element at depth d
equal to obj. With no depth, it searches depth 1 and returns the bare
keys of the matches in encounter order: (where (:a :b :b :c) :b) is
(2 3) and a single match (where (:a :b :c) :b) is (2). With an explicit
non-negative integer depth, it returns one path per occurrence, each
path a list of d keys: (where ((1 2) (3 2)) 2 depth=2) is
((1 2) (2 2)) and (where (:a :b :c) :b depth=1) is ((2)). At depth=0
the subject is the only candidate and its sole key is the whole-form key 0,
so the result is ((0)) when the subject equals obj and () otherwise.
depth=:all searches every depth and returns one path per occurrence, each of
its own length: (where (:a :b (:a :b) :c) :b depth=:all) is ((2) (3 2)).
No match is () in every mode. Results are plain (not held); splice a path
into get, with, or update-in: (get coll (first (where …))...).

A scalar is its own sole sequence for the accessors: (get 10 1) is 10,
descending past a scalar stays on it, and out-of-bounds indices throw, so a
scalar participates naturally in collection operations ((push 10 11) is
(10 11)). This is an accessor convention, not a rewrite: a written
container is never collapsed, so 10, (10), and ((10)) are three distinct
forms and (eq? 10 (10)) is false. A one-element form reduces only when a
def (or builtin) matches it. The sole canonicalization is the empty form:
() and naught are the same singleton at every depth, so (same? () naught)
is true and no container ever embeds an empty container.

Holding is structural, not a flag: the canonical hold is a container whose
first element is the ordinary symbol ', (' a b c). ' is an ordinary
symbol character (a'b is a symbol), but a symbol may not begin with it —
except the bare ' itself. There is no separate held bit on a form, and a held
form is an ordinary value everywhere. 'x is reader sugar for (' x) when x
is a scalar ('a, '5, ':x, '"abc"); the container spelling '(…) is
a parse error — write (' …).

Literal Forms: a hold holds each of its elements as written, so
(' a b c) holds three elements and (' (a b c)) holds one container. '5
and ':a stay held as well. A hold of exactly one scalar prints with the
quote ('a, '5, ':a); any other hold prints literally ((' a b c),
(' f x=1)). (hold e…) is the reserved alias that reduces to (' e…).
A held form does not reduce — it is data. (unhold (' a b c)) drops the head
and evaluates the remaining content, giving (a b c).

Unquoting (~): ~e is sugar for (preval e), a reserved special form
that evaluates e eagerly wherever it appears. Inside a held form each
~e is filled in with the reduced form of e at every depth (a nested hold
fills its own holes): (hold (a ~(1 + 2))) reduces to (' (a 3)). ~ is
not the runtime unhold operation — that is the ordinary call (unhold x),
which evaluates a held form’s content. Use lift (below) to build a quoted
form explicitly from literal and evaluated parts. A hole may be a map value
((f x=~(1 + 2)) is (f x=3), and x=~y is the same hole in atom form),
and a trailing ... splices the hole’s value into the enclosing sequence
rather than its operand ((f ~(1 2 3)...) is (f 1 2 3)).

Access: because a hold is an ordinary form, the hold-blind accessors see it
as one — (first (' a b c)) is ' and (count (' a b c)) is 4. get
indexes the form as written, so for a held form index 1 is the ' head and
index 2 is the first element of its content: (get (' f a b) 2) is f and
(get (' f x=1) :x) is 1. Pass hold=true to make the root hold
transparent — the path then indexes the content, intermediate values are not
reduced, and the result is held: (get (' f (1 + 2)) 2 hold=true) is
(' 1 + 2). This works for any form that keeps its arguments as data
((get (part add 10) 2 hold=true) is 'add).
(with form k1 v1 … hold=true) is the inverse: it replaces the subform at
each path with its value, inserted without its own hold and not evaluated —
(with (' a b c) 2 (' 1 + 1) hold=true) is (' a (1 + 1) c). (held? x)
tests whether x is a held form, and (held? form k…) tests the subpart at
that path (hold=true makes the root hold transparent first). lower pushes
holds toward the leaves and lift lifts them back to the root
((lift (' ' a x ' b)) → (' a <value-of-x> b)).

The hold- family: every collection operation that takes a primary form
has a hold- version — hold-get, hold-nth, hold-with, hold-wout,
hold-push, hold-push-in, hold-join, hold-join-in, hold-update,
hold-thread, hold-held?. These treat the primary form’s root hold as
transparent (the operation is on the content), let inserted held values
contribute their content, and return the result held:
(hold-get (' 1 2 3) 2) is (' 2). Each takes hold= to select the result’s
heldness ((hold-get (' 1 2 3) 2 hold=false) is 2), and the plain version
accepts hold=true for the same treatment ((get (1 2 3) 2 hold=true) is
(' 2)).

In addition to immutable atom types, there is a mutable type that form
objects are able to contain. All mutable objects are simple
pointers/references automatically synchronized across threads in a fashion
similar to Clojure’s ref objects (implemented via AirDB.jl).

Mutables can be created using (mut). Mutables automatically vanish during
queries, but can be updated using (set! ...) which traverses forms and updates
the deepest mutable object on the path. For example, if f equals
(1 (2 (mut (3 (4 5))))), then (set! f 2 2 2 2 6) updates the mutable at
(f 2 2) such that its value has been updated to set its position 2 2 to the
value 6. (value m), (get m), and (get m 0) all read the mutable’s value;
(swap! m f args…) (alias alter!) replaces it with (f value args…) in one
transaction and returns the new value, so a lost update is impossible.

Every operation that edits a mutable in a transaction ends in !: set!,
swap!, alter!, chmod!, and chown!. mut does not, because it creates
rather than edits a volatile. (reset! actor value) replaces an actor’s value
directly (see 

Delays, actors, and promises); a
mutable is written with set!.

(mut value filter=… finalize=…) attaches Air’s filter and finalizer. Both are
kept as written and stored in the mutable’s metadata, so they survive a reload.
A replacement rule (?x -> …) is applied as a function; any other form is
evaluated with _ bound to the value, so filter=(if (_ < 0) 0 _) clamps at
zero. A filter runs on every write (including the value passed to mut) and its
result is stored; a finalizer runs after the body of the writing transaction and
before it commits, and its result replaces the value. Because the finalizer runs
in the transaction’s finalizing state, volatiles cannot be written from it.
(set-filter! m fn) and (set-finalize! m fn) replace them later (naught
removes one).

(watch m key fn) registers fn to run as (fn key m old new) at the end of
the body of the outermost transaction that writes m, before it commits. The
watch runs as the user who registered it, in the namespace where it was
registered, and once per mutable per transaction (with the transaction’s final
value). Its writes are part of the same transaction, so a retry reruns it; a
raise from it aborts the transaction, while a throw is deferred like any
throw caught outside (see tx below). Watches are stored in the mutable’s
metadata and survive a reload; a watch function must be self-contained (a
replacement rule, not a code fragment using _). Installing a watch needs
watch and read on the mutable; watch is owner-only by default.
(unwatch m key…) removes one watch or all of them, and (watches m) returns
the held watch tables.

(tx body…) evaluates the body inside one STM transaction and yields its last
value. It accepts the full do block grammar — :let/let=, catch=/throw,
except, handle/notify, and finally — all prepared and run inside the
transaction. Air’s transactions join rather than nest: tx joins an open
transaction, so the outermost tx is the commit/rollback boundary (namespace,
load-air, a logic-set edit, and set! are transactional too). An error that
escapes it aborts every write made since it began and propagates, even if an
outer block catches it; an error caught by the tx’s own except commits. A
throw caught by the tx’s own catch= commits. A throw that escapes the tx to an
outer catch= is deferred until after the commit: watches run as usual, the
transaction commits, and the signal is rethrown (a retried attempt discards it).
Watches run at the end of that outermost transaction body, so their writes commit
or roll back with it.

(sandbox body…) evaluates the same block grammar in a transaction that is
never committed: it yields the body’s value and discards every write, so a
def, val, mut, fact, rule, or namespace created inside it is gone
afterwards. It is the way to try something out — a rule you are not sure about,
a namespace edit you want to test — without touching the namespace. Because Air’s
transactions join rather than nest, the body runs in a transaction of its own on
a private task (the caller waits for it), which means it cannot abort a
transaction around it and it reads committed state rather than an enclosing
transaction’s staged writes. A throw still reaches an enclosing catch= and a
notify an enclosing handle; side effects outside the database (a file write,
open-airdb) are not undone.

Three relations are distinct:

(same? a b) is object identity (===).

(eq? a b) is equivalence. Two scalars are equivalent when they have the
same value and the same type, so (eq? 1 1.0) is false even though
(== 1 1.0) is true. A signed zero is one value under equivalence
((eq? -0.0 0.0) is true) and NaN is equivalent to itself. Two containers
are equivalent when their sequences are
elementwise equivalent and their maps hold equivalent values under the same
keys (map order is irrelevant). A mutable (a volatile), an actor, and a
promise are equivalent only to themselves; an extern follows its own
isequal, so two separately compiled equal regex values are equivalent while
two tasks’ promises are not. A delay is equivalent when its type and its
serialization agree — equivalence never forces one. Everything immutable
is therefore comparable by
value, even when it points at a mutable: the mutable part contributes only
its identity.

(== a b) is content equality, the numeric-friendly relation used by the
arithmetic comparisons ((== 1 1.0) is true, as are (== -0.0 0.0) and
(== (f 1) (f 1.0))). It is AirDB’s ==, under which a NaN is equal to
nothing, just as in Julia; eq? is the relation that treats NaN as equal to
itself.

(hash x) follows eq?: equivalent forms hash alike, and the hash never
descends into a mutable object (a volatile hashes by its identity), so any
immutable form is hashable even when it contains one. Two forms that hash alike
need not be equivalent, but equivalent forms always hash alike, which is what a
memoization table or a keyed map needs.

A process starts with one private in-memory database holding the air root
(.air, .sys, .lib, .main, and the system user records). (open-airdb name opts…) opens an AirDB database, roots a namespace at name in it, and
attaches @ to that root for the calling task. From Julia, Env(db = d) selects
the process database — the store behind ., .main, and a system user’s
home — and does not change the database of any opened root:(open-airdb .work memory=true)      ; an in-memory database (as in the tests)
(open-airdb .work dbname="air" user="air" host="localhost" port=5432)
(open-airdb .work url="postgresql://air@localhost/air" create=true)

option

meaning

memory=true

a fresh in-memory database

url= / conninfo=

a libpq connection string, passed through verbatim

dbname= user= host= port= password= sslmode=

a PostgreSQL connection (host defaults to localhost, port to 5432)

create=true

create the schema (create_database); the PostgreSQL database itself must exist

create=false

open an existing schema only

(absent)

try to open, then create

A bare name is relative to the current namespace (so air’s (open-airdb work …) roots .main.work); an explicit .path or @.path is absolute.
Opening requires write on the containing namespace, and a root may not be
placed over an existing namespace or where a database is already open. Unless
the opener is air, opening writes the opener’s user record into the database;
an admin’s status carries over. A newly created root is owned by its opener.

A namespace at or under an opened root lives in that database (the
longest-prefixed open root wins), so (namespace .work.util …) is durable
there. @ addresses the same root: with .work open, @.util.f is
.work.util.f. Opening a database inside another ((open-airdb .work.sub …))
creates a distinct database that owns the namespaces at or under .work.sub,
with its own users and permissions.

Database users are separate from system users. (create-user :bob) while
attached writes @.user.bob into the attached database; (users) lists that
database’s users (air included); and a permission map in a database may name
only one of its own users (or _), so (chmod! .work read=(mallory=true))
raises a bad-user error. A user of another database is likewise not a valid
principal.

Because namespaces in a database are persisted as linked volatiles, a value
assigned there must be storable: it may not embed a volatile from another
database. Storing .main’s mutable or the .air namespace raises
(error :un-storable target) instead of writing an unresolvable link. mut inside a
database namespace creates its mutable in that same database.

(close-airdb name) flushes and closes the database, removes its root namespace
from the parent, and detaches @ (returning it to .) when it pointed at that
root. Closing a database also closes any database rooted beneath it. From Julia,
open_airdb!(env, path, db) roots an already-opened database — the way the
tests use MemoryDatabase — and close_airdb!(env, path) closes it.

The process database also holds .sys.ssh.<key> for every SSH server that has
been started under that name: private and public vals holding the host key
and a config mapping recording the owner and key type. .sys is readable only
by air, so the record is reached through the SSH builtins
((ssh-host-key key)), never by a path; it is what makes a reopened server the
same host. See 

SSH access.

A form’s database is the database of the namespace it is written in, never
an ambient store chosen by the environment. The system namespaces (., .air,
.sys, .lib, .main, and a system user’s home) live in the process database;
a namespace at or under an opened root lives in that root’s database. mut,
logic-set, the named-form operations, form-at, and from-json all follow
this one rule, so a mutable made in .main belongs to the process store even
while @ points elsewhere, and storing it in a database namespace raises
(error :un-storable …).

AirDB registers a name for a volatile, giving a form a durable, database-wide
handle:(named-form :counter create=true value=3)   ; create and name a new volatile
(named-form :counter)                       ; the same volatile
(value (named-form :counter))               ; 3
(named-form :counter create=false)          ; raises when the name is absent
(named-form :counter create=naught)         ; naught when the name is absent
(named-form :alias create=true value=(named-form :counter))  ; an alias
(name-form! :other (named-form :counter))   ; repoint an existing name
(named-forms)                               ; (alias=(mut 3) counter=(mut 3) …)

A name may be a keyword, a raw symbol, or a string; :counter and "counter"
agree, and the leading colon of a keyword is stripped, so (named-form :counter) registers counter. Names beginning air/ are reserved for air’s
own bookkeeping and neither appear in named-forms nor may be created.
value= may be an ordinary form or an existing volatile of the same database,
in which case the name becomes an alias for it (no new form is made). A
created form records its history unless history=false. The name table is
transactional: a creation or repointing joins the enclosing transaction, so it
is retried or discarded with it, and a failed transaction leaves no name behind.

Creating a name publishes an entry from the current namespace, so it needs
write there (and a user record in a database); a lookup needs read on the
named form. A new named form is owned by its creator with the default owner-only
ACL. named-forms lists the names the caller may read. name-form! may claim a
free name with write in the namespace; repointing an existing name instead
needs write on the form currently named (or on the database root, for a
database administrator).

A logic set is a named volatile holding facts, rules, and their provenance.
There are two ways to reach one.

A standalone set is named explicitly: (logic-set :s) is (named-form :s)
whose value has the logic-set shape, and every operation takes it as its target.
Its ACL is the old mapping — mutating the set (assert, retract, revise,
revise-fact, and logic) needs write, and every query (facts, rules,
why, and query) needs read, as does opening the set by name.

Every namespace is implicitly a logic set. (assert .foo (p 1)) writes into
the set of .foo; with no target, (assert (p 1)) writes into the current
namespace, so a bare assert inside (namespace .foo …) or while .foo is
current edits .foo. facts, rules, why, query, revise, retract,
revise-fact, defrule, and ingest accept a namespace the same way. The set
is stored as the hidden named form air/logic/<path> (air/logic at the root)
in the namespace’s own database, so it persists, shares the namespace’s access
control, and never appears in named-forms; air/ is reserved, so it cannot be
opened by name. The set is created lazily by the first fact or rule write; a
namespace with no set reads as an empty set, and a read never creates one.(namespace .app)
(assert .app (depends :app :lib1))       ; creates air/logic/app
(assert .app (rule (depends ?x ?y) :> (needs ?x ?y)))
(facts .app)                             ; => (' (depends :app :lib1) (needs :app :lib1))
(query .app (needs ?x ?y))               ; => ((x=:app y=:lib1))

(facts target) and (rules target) return one held list of the facts or
rules — (' (depends :app :lib1) (needs :app :lib1)), and (') for an empty
set — whose elements are the facts themselves, unheld, so the list is ordinary
data that a def cannot rewrite while the hold keeps evaluating it inert.

The four fact/rule permissions gate these operations on a namespace
(readfact/writefact/readrule/writerule; see


permissions); a rule form asserted or retracted needs the
…rule permission, and why needs both read permissions.

(query [target] pattern…) returns every distinct satisfier of a rule-like
condition block as a plain list of maps, in first-seen order: (query .app (depends ?x ?y)). The patterns are the rule engine’s conditions — an implicit
conjunction, (not p) for negation, and infix and — but there are no
instructions and no accumulators. A pattern whose head is rule searches the
rule universe; every other pattern searches the facts. A satisfier with no
bindings is (naught), and no satisfier is naught. (defrule conditions… instructions…) builds a (rule …) form from its raw arguments and asserts it
into the current target, returning the rule. (ingest source) copies a source’s
base facts and rules into the current target in one transaction and saturates it,
so derived facts are rederived rather than copied; it checks exactly the
permissions it uses, all before mutating anything. Live propagation from a source
to its dependants is not implemented (depend is a tombstone) and is tracked in
TODO.md.

Every operation outside a logic block is its own transaction, so separate
asserts commit independently; (logic target body…) collects the body’s edits
and applies them as one event, and any enclosing (tx …) also joins them.

(sync) blocks until every write committed before the call has reached the
database; (sync target) targets a namespace or volatile instead of the current
namespace’s database. It is a barrier, not a drain: it queues a flush behind
the writes already scheduled, so writes that other tasks schedule afterward do
not delay it, and the sequential writer cannot be starved by continuing
activity. (status) returns (pending=N error=naught): the number of updates
scheduled but not yet written, and the last writer error. Both are also
.air.sys.sync and .air.sys.status.

Air defers an actor message sent inside an open transaction until that
transaction commits, so a sync placed inside a namespace, load-air, or
other transaction cannot include that transaction’s own writes. It flushes
every write already scheduled and returns; the block’s writes are scheduled when
the block commits, so call (sync) outside the block to make them durable. A
MemoryDatabase has nothing to flush, so its sync returns at once.

(form-id volatile) returns the form’s UUID as a string. (form-at id) returns
the volatile with that id in the current database without loading its body; when
no such form is in the database, reading the handle raises (error :form-not-found id). (loaded? volatile) reports whether the body has been read into memory,
and (history volatile) whether the form records its history.

(to-json value) encodes a form as JSON text and (from-json text) decodes it
in the current database. The codec is AirDB’s: numbers and booleans are JSON
scalars, naught is null, a string is a JSON string carrying its reader quote
('hi), a keyword is a JSON string carrying its colon ("::x"), a form is the
pair [sequence, map], and a volatile is the link string "@uuid". Links are
never expanded, so a cyclic structure encodes; from-json resolves each link
through the current database, and a link to a missing form raises
(error :form-not-found id). An extern encodes by type and id ({"extern": …, "id": …}) and reads back through the database’s resource registry. The
database reference forms have their own encodings: an actor is "!uuid", a
promise is "~uuid" until it is delivered (then it encodes as its value), and a
delay is {"delay": ":air", "form": <the cell's link>} — never forced by
encoding. A form bound for a database may embed only volatiles, actors, promises,
and delays of that same database; anything else raises
(error :un-storable target).

Printing is cycle-safe on the same terms: a volatile that contains itself prints
the inner occurrence opaquely as #<volatile uuid> instead of recursing.

JSON has no infinity or NaN, so AirDB writes a non-finite float as a marked
string: Inf is "#inf", -Inf is "#-inf", and NaN is "#nan". The #
marker cannot be confused with a string ('), a symbol (:), or a link (@),
and a literal string that looks like one is still a string, so (to-json inf)
is the JSON string "#inf" while (to-json "#inf") is "'#inf". Such a value
flushes to any database, including the .air constants inf and nan.

The rest of the numeric tower has a marker too, so an exact value never degrades
on the way through JSON: a BigInt is "#big:…", a rational "#rat:n/d" (or
"#bigrat:n/d"), and a BigFloat "#bigfloat:<bits>:…". See


Numbers.

Air features a pattern-matched, structural error system integrated directly into
its core evaluation engine, replacing traditional class-based exception
hierarchies. Errors are ordinary forms, so they can be stored, matched, compared,
and printed like any other value.

An error object is a form whose first element is the ordinary symbol
error:(error :io "Connection lost")
(error)                    # the empty error
(error :arg :a x=1)        # the map is part of the object

The reducer never evaluates an error object or any of its elements: error is
an inert head, so (error :io (+ 1 2)) is the unevaluated form
(error :io (+ 1 2)) at any depth. The first element after the head is
conventionally the error type (a keyword), but air never inspects it; the type
is optional and purely conventional. error cannot be given a reduction rule.

raise is a special form that constructs an error object and throws it.(raise :io "Connection lost" path="/tmp/x")

Arguments are evaluated. (raise :io (+ 1 2)) raises
(error :io 3). Map entries are evaluated too.

No type is required. (raise), (raise :io), and (raise "oops") are
all legal; they raise (error), (error :io), and (error "oops").

The first slot is not special. (raise :io "x") raises (error :io "x")
and (raise "a" "b") raises (error "a" "b").

A single error object is raised exactly. If raise has exactly one
positional argument and no options and that argument evaluates to an
(error …) object, the object is thrown as it is — its elements are not
re-evaluated or copied:(raise (error :io (+ 1 2)))        # throws (error :io (+ 1 2))
(raise (error :io) "abc")          # (error (error :io) "abc")

Adding any option (or a second argument) makes raise rebuild an object, so
the error object becomes the first payload element.

records.content:
do is the language’s block form and subsumes the old try: it evaluates a
body with optional binding, error clauses, signal handlers, and a finalizer.
tx accepts exactly the same grammar and runs it inside one transaction.(do
    let=(scale=2)                       # a lexical block scope
    :let (x=(compute scale))            # a textual binding inside the body
    (some-function x)                   # body…
  (except (:io ??data)                  # matches the content of (error :io …)
    (print "I/O failed: " data)
    :handled)
  (except (:arg ?x \ symbol?)
    :bad-argument)
  (except ?err                          # a bare wildcard binds the whole object
    (print "Unrecognized error: " err)
    reraise)                            # resume it (see below)
  (handle (:progress ?pct)              # a notified signal runs here and
    (print pct "%"))                    # execution continues after notify
  (finally
    (print "done")))

A block is(do options… body… (except pattern body…)… (handle pattern body…)… (finally body…)?)

The only options are let= and catch=. The body runs left to right, and the
clauses that follow it may be except and handle in any order; at most one
finally may appear, and it must be last. A bare (catch …) clause is an
error: write catch= for a throw tag or except for an error pattern.
except/handle outside a block remain ordinary data.

The block’s value is the last body value (naught for an empty body), a caught
throw value, or the matching except/handle body’s value. finally’s value
is discarded. Block setup — the let= values and the catch= tags — runs
before the body; a failure there is not handled by the same block’s clauses and
does not run its finally (an outer block can still handle it).

records.content:
A level-1 bare :let in the body consumes the next body form as a let
binding form; the remaining body forms become its body. Markers nest left to
right, need not be first, and a marker in the final body position is inert
data. :let is the same textual let as elsewhere: its names are substituted
into the rest of the body, and they are not visible to except, handle,
or finally.

let= instead wraps the whole block in one lexical scope, visible in the
body, clause bodies, signal handlers, and finally, and outermost relative to
any :let markers. Its groups feed one another exactly as let’s do, but as a
scope it does not rewrite inside a hold or a computed key.(do let=(a=1) :let (a=2) a)        ; => 2
(do let=(a=5) :let (a=2) (raise :x) (except (:x) a))   ; => 5

records.content:
Content matching. An except pattern is matched against the content
of the error object: the object without its error head, keeping its map.
(except (:io ?msg) …) therefore matches (error :io "x") with
msg = "x", and (except () …) matches (error).

Bare wildcards bind the object. A pattern that is a single non-rest
wildcard (?e, ?) is matched against the whole error object, so the handler
can inspect or re-raise it. Use (except (:io ??data) …) to capture the
content’s sequence and map.

First match wins. Clauses are tested top to bottom; the first matching
clause runs and later clauses are skipped.

Escaping. If no clause matches, the error continues propagating. A new
error raised inside a handler also escapes the block; it is not offered to
later clauses.

Empty body. A matching except with no body evaluates to naught and
consumes the error.

Host exceptions. A non-air exception is matched through the error object
air builds for it ((error :internal message), or a specific head such as
:form-not-found), and is rethrown unchanged when no clause matches.

reraise is a reserved bare symbol (it cannot be bound by let, def, or a
pattern). When the final value of an except body is reraise, the
original error resumes as if that clause had not fired: later clauses still get
a chance to match it, and if none handles it, it escapes the block. Side
effects performed before the reraise are kept.(do (raise :io "x")
  (except (:io ?m) reraise)      ; log here, then let the next clause see it
  (except ?e (print e)))

records.content:
catch= makes a throw return from the block early:(let (x=-1)
  (do catch=:tag
      (if (< x 0) (throw :tag :undef))
      (sqrt x)))                 ; => :undef

catch=true is the literal tag true; catch=:tag is one tag;
catch=(tag1 tag2…) is a list. Tags are held literals, not forms and not
patterns: a symbol is not evaluated. ~expr is the only escape and must
reduce to a scalar. Any other form is an error, as are an empty catch= and
a catch= with map entries.

(throw value) means (throw true value); (throw) is
(throw true naught); (throw tag value) uses a held or computed tag. The
value is evaluated. Extra arguments or map options are errors.

At a throw, the innermost active catch= scope with a matching tag accepts
it. A block catches only signals aimed at its own scope, so same-tag nesting
is unambiguous and other signals pass through. A throw from an except
body is caught by the same block’s catch=; one from finally is not (its
catch scope is already closed), though an outer block can still catch it.

With no matching catch, the throw is immediately the ordinary error
(error :uncaught-throw tag value), raised from the throw form’s position.
except clauses therefore never see a throw signal; they see only that
error once no catch matches.

records.content:
A signal object is a form headed by the ordinary symbol signal. Like an
error object it is a constant: it never reduces, at any depth.(signal :progress 40)

(notify data…) evaluates its positional arguments and map values. With
exactly one positional argument, no map entries, and a (signal …) value, it
dispatches that object unchanged; otherwise it dispatches the freshly built
signal. Handlers are searched from the innermost active block to the outermost,
and top to bottom within a block; the first match wins. A handler pattern
matches the signal’s content (the object without its head, keeping the map),
and a bare non-rest wildcard binds the whole signal object.

A matching handler runs at the notify site in its defining block’s scope (the
block’s let= scope, plus the pattern bindings). Its value becomes notify’s
value and execution continues. A handler is dynamically scoped but lexically
evaluated: it is registered at block entry, works for a notify written
before the handle clause, and disappears when the block exits. An error
raised by a handler follows the context in which the notify ran.

With no matching handler, notify raises (error :unhandled-signal signal)
from the notify form. (notify-or default data…) is the same, except default
is held and evaluated only when nothing matches; it is not part of the signal.(do (notify :progress 40)
  (handle (:progress ?pct) (+ pct 1)))     ; => 41
(do (notify-or :none :progress 40)
  (handle (:progress ?pct) pct))           ; => 40

Catch scopes and handler scopes are task-local and do not cross a (task …)
boundary: a notify in a task with no local handler is an :unhandled-signal
error, and an unmatched throw becomes an :uncaught-throw error rethrown by
await.

records.content:
finally always runs — after normal completion, after a matched except, after
a caught throw, after a reraise, and while an error or throw escapes. It may
appear without any other clause, must be last, and there may be at most one. Its
value is discarded. The block’s handle scope is still active while it runs,
but its catch=/except are closed. If it raises or throws, that condition
replaces the result or the condition already in flight, and a replaced error
becomes the new error’s automatic from (see below).

records.content:
A def body (and a val body, which is evaluated once at definition time) is
this same block. It takes let= and catch=, level-1 :let markers, and
trailing except/handle/finally clauses; several body forms are evaluated
in sequence as by do. Everything above applies unchanged: an error from the
body can be handled by its own except, a throw by its own catch=, and a
finally always runs.

tx=true (the only def-specific option besides memoize=) runs the whole
body as a tx instead of a do:(def (store ?x) tx=true (write-something x) (raise :disk-full))
(do (store 5) (except (:disk-full) 1))
; => 1, and the write is rolled back

(def (safe-store ?x) tx=true (write-something x) (raise :disk-full)
  (except (:disk-full) :failed))
(safe-store 5)
; => :failed, and the write commits

tx=false is the default, an ordinary block with no transaction. A memoized
body caches only a successful result; an error or throw passes through and
stores nothing.

A do with no catch=, except, handle, or finally keeps its last body
form in tail position (including when it uses :let/let=), so a tail call
through it does not grow the stack. Any condition-handling feature makes the
block run eagerly, and tx is never a tail form.

records.content:
try has been removed. Rewrite (try body… (except …)… (finally …)) as
(do body… (except …)… (finally …)); it is a tombstone that raises an error.

Python distinguishes implicit context (__context__) from an explicitly
declared cause (__cause__); air uses the map options from= and cause=.

from is automatic context. A raise inside an except handler (or a
finally with an error in flight) records the error being handled as
from=:(do (raise :disk-full) (except (:disk-full) (raise :save-failed)))
; => (error :save-failed from=(error :disk-full))

An explicit from= overrides the automatic value, and from=naught
suppresses it. Raising an error object exactly (the single-object rule) does
not add from.

cause is explicit only. Use cause= when one error transforms another:
(raise :save-failed cause=(error :disk-full)).

Both are ordinary map entries, matchable like any other; ?* and ?? capture
them, while ?& does not.

showerror prints the chain recursively, labeling an explicit cause
direct cause: and an automatic context during handling of::air error: (error :save-failed)
  ...
direct cause:
  (error :disk-full)

The walk is depth-limited to 16 links to stop cycles.

A non-air exception raised by the host (bad index, closed file, permission
denial, parse failure, …) is presented to except as an error object too,
conventionally (error :internal message). Air conditions use their own heads
(:permission-denied, :extern-expired, :database-error, :form-not-found,
:proxy-unresolved, :un-storable), all matched through their content.(do (get (1 2) 5) (except (:internal ?msg) msg))

Error handling interacts directly with Air’s Software Transactional Memory
(Air.jl) and persistence layer (AirDB.jl):

Uncaught errors abort. An error that escapes its enclosing transaction
boundary triggers an automatic STM transaction abort and rollback,
preventing partial or corrupted state changes from committing. This is true
even when an outer block catches the error: the abort has already happened.

Caught errors commit. An error intercepted and handled inside the except
clause of a do/tx running inside the transaction does not force a
rollback, letting the transaction recover or handle validation failures
gracefully.

Throws commit first. A throw caught by a block inside the
transaction returns normally and commits. A throw that escapes the
transaction to an outer catch= is deferred: the body returns normally (so
writes are not staged as an abort), watches run as on a normal exit, the
transaction commits, and only then is the signal rethrown. If the transaction
fails and Air retries, the deferred throw from the failed attempt is
discarded and the body runs again, so the throw may never complete.

Handlers run in the transaction. A handler notified while the transaction
is open is ordinary code in that transaction: its writes are transactional
and roll back with an abort. A watch error aborts; a watch throw replaces a
pending throw (the last one wins). Exceptions raised by a finally or by
finalizers/commit are outside the deferral and abort.

A tx=true definition is a boundary. The body of such a def (or val)
is an explicit tx, so an escaping error aborts the body’s writes and an
error caught by the body’s own except, or a throw caught by its own
catch=, commits. Nested inside another transaction, it joins it rather than
opening a second boundary.

Forms are data, so a position is not part of a form; the reader records the
character span of each container it parses, and a loader (load-air, a library
init.air, or the CLI) installs that record task-locally while it evaluates the
forms. Positions are best-effort: an environment that evaluates a bare form — a
REPL call, a test — has no source record and reports no position.

Two decorations are attached to an error as frames, innermost first:

The top-level form during whose evaluation the error escaped, from the
loader’s span record.

The definition site of the def whose body was executing, from the
src= entry that def/val store in the namespace entry’s body (the body is
gated by read like any other; diagnostics read it internally). The innermost
rule context wins, so an error inside g’s body reported while f calls g
describes g’s definition, not f’s.

A frame is the map form (name=… line=… col=… text=…), where name is the file
path (or <interactive>), line/col are 1-based, and text is the exact
source text of the form. showerror prints the innermost frame as
(at name:line:col) followed by the first line of its source text; a parse
error carries name:  before its message. The decoration never changes the
error object that except matches.

(trace body…) evaluates its body and yields the last value. If an error
escapes, it yields the final data form(:trace (error :oops 1) frames=((name="/tmp/t.air" line=1 col=1 text="(def (bad ?x) (raise :oops x))")))

instead of throwing: the first element is the error object an except would
see, and frames lists the source frames known for it (() when none). The
result is final, so neither the error object nor the frames are re-reduced;
nested trace forms simply see the outer result as data. Use it to inspect a
failure without stopping a load or test.

Worked solutions to the 25 problems in the 

problem set, written in air and
checked against the interpreter. Each entry gives the air code and a status:

✓ — works as written.

⚠ — works, with a caveat noted inline.

✗ — cannot be written with the current system; the blocking gap is named.

Everything here runs against an in-memory database (MemoryDatabase), so no
Postgres is needed; only the STM examples in Tier 4 need env.db.

Two syntax notes that the examples rely on: a :name is a keyword (inert
data), while a hold is a container headed by the symbol ' — (' a b c) —
and 'x is sugar for (' x) when x is a scalar, so (' a b) stays held as
data. Inside a hold, ~e (sugar for (preval e)) is substituted with the value
of e ((let (x=2) (' a ~x b)) → (' a 2 b); a let, however, substitutes its
names textually, so (let (x=2) (' a x b)) → (' a 2 b) too). (let (x=1 y=2) body…) binds in parallel and substitutes the values into the body before
evaluating it; a sequence of mappings, (let ((a=1) (b=2)) body…), lets each
group feed the next. (get c i) is the one accessor: an integer indexes a
sequence (1-based), a keyword a map, so a held form’s content starts at index 2
((get (' f a b) 2) is f). hold=true makes the root hold transparent, keeps
the extracted part held, and walks the path without reducing the intermediates;
(with form k1 … kn val hold=true) is the inverse, replacing a subpart with
val inserted without its own hold. The hold- family (hold-get,
hold-with, …) is the same treatment with the result held, and >> builds a
pipeline with _ as the placeholder ((x >> (_ + 1) (f _))).

2D grids are nested forms; get indexes them and the neighbour sum uses for
over the 3×3 offset window:(def (cell ?g ?r ?c)
  (if (or (r < 1) (c < 1) (r > (count g)) (c > (count (get g 1)))) 0
    (let (v=(get (get g r) c)) (if (naught? v) 0 v))))

(def (neighbours ?g ?r ?c)
  (reduce + 0 (for (dr (range -1 2) dc (range -1 2)
                       :if (not (and (dr == 0) (dc == 0))))
                   (cell g (r + dr) (c + dc)))))

(def grid ((1 0 0) (0 1 0) (0 0 1)))
(neighbours grid 2 2)   # => 2
(neighbours grid 3 3)   # => 1

get is 1-based on a sequence, so the bounds test is 1 ≤ r ≤ (count g) and
1 ≤ c ≤ (count (get g 1)); the caller passes 1-based coordinates. The centre
of the diagonal grid touches both other 1s (2 neighbours); the bottom-right
corner touches only the centre (1).

records.content:
Unification is written in air itself: terms are ordinary forms held raw by the
rule parameters, variables are wildcards (?x), and a substitution is a map from
:x to its value.# ---- Mini-Prolog: unification ------------------------------------------------

(def (deref ?t ?s) hold=(t)
  (if (and (wildcard? t) (haskey s (keyword (name t))))
      (let (v=(get s (keyword (name t))))
        (deref v s))
      t))

(def (bind-var ?v ?t ?s)
  (join s ~(keyword (name v))=t))

(def (term-equal ?a ?b) hold=(a b)
  (if (seq? a)
      (if (seq? b)
          (if (== (count a) (count b))
              (loop (i 1)
                (if (i > (count a))
                    true
                    (let (ai=(get a i) bi=(get b i))
                      (if (term-equal ai bi)
                          (recur (i + 1))
                          false))))
              false)
          false)
      (if (seq? b) false (eq? (unhold a) (unhold b)))))

(def (unify-list ?xs ?ys ?i ?s) hold=(xs ys)
  (if (i > (count xs))
      s
      (let (xi=(get xs i) yi=(get ys i))
        (let (s2=(unify xi yi s))
  (if (eq? s2 :fail)
              :fail
              (unify-list xs ys (i + 1) s2))))))

(def (unify ?a ?b ?s) hold=(a b)
  (let (da=(deref a s) db=(deref b s))
    (if (and (wildcard? da) (wildcard? db) (term-equal da db))
        s
        (if (wildcard? da)
            (bind-var da db s)
            (if (wildcard? db)
                (bind-var db da s)
                (if (and (seq? da) (seq? db))
                    (if (== (count da) (count db))
                        (unify-list da db 1 s)
                        :fail)
                    (if (term-equal da db) s :fail)))))))

# ---- Mini-Prolog: resolution -------------------------------------------------

(def (rename-term ?t ?tag) hold=(t)
  (if (wildcard? t)
      (symbol (str "?" (name t) tag))
      (if (seq? t)
          (map (?e -> (rename-term e tag)) t)
          t)))

(def (push-goals ?q ?b)
  (loop (i (- (count b) 1) acc q)
    (if (i < 2)
        acc
        (recur (i - 1) (push acc (get b i))))))

(def (vars ?t ?acc) hold=(t)
  (if (wildcard? t)
      (if (member? t acc) acc (push acc t))
      (if (seq? t)
          (reduce ((?acc ?e) -> (vars e acc)) acc t)
          acc)))

(def (project ?vset ?s)
  (reduce ((?acc ?v) -> (join acc ~(keyword (name v))=(deref v s)))
          ()
          (drop-first 2 vset)))

(def (sol-count ?ss) (if (symbol? ss) 0 (- (count ss) 1)))
(def (sol-get ?ss ?i) (get ss (i + 1)))
(def (sol-add ?ss ?s) (if (symbol? ss) (sols s) (push ss s)))
(def (sol-merge ?a ?b)
  (loop (i 1 acc a)
    (if (i > (sol-count b))
        acc
        (recur (i + 1) (sol-add acc (sol-get b i))))))

(def (solve-clauses ?i ?acc ?g ?q ?db ?tag ?s ?vset)
  (loop (i i acc acc)
    (if (i > (count db))
        acc
        (let (c=(get db i))
          (let (tag2=(str tag "_" i))
            (let (h0=(get c :head))
              (let (b0=(get c :body))
                (let (h=(rename-term h0 tag2))
                  (let (b=(rename-term b0 tag2))
                    (let (s2=(unify g h s))
                      (recur (i + 1)
                             (if (eq? s2 :fail)
                                 acc
                                 (sol-merge acc (solve-q (push-goals q b) db tag2 s2 vset))))))))))))))

(def (solve-q ?q ?db ?tag ?s ?vset)
  (if (== (count q) 2)
      (sol-add sols (project vset s))
      (let (n=(count q))
        (let (g=(get q n))
  (let (q2=(wout q n))
  (solve-clauses 2 sols g q2 db tag s vset))))))

(def (solve ?goal ?db) hold=(goal)
  (solve-q (goals :done goal) db "" () (vars goal (vs :done))))

A database is a clauses form of head=/body= maps; each body is a goals
form headed by the goals marker and ending with a :done sentinel, which the
goal stack uses to detect the end of the search. The query is a raw term —
solve’s hold=goal parameter receives it exactly as written, so it is not
reduced:(let (db=(clauses
          (head=(parent :abe :bob) body=(goals :done))
          (head=(parent :bob :carl) body=(goals :done))
          (head=(ancestor ?x ?y) body=(goals (parent ?x ?y) :done))
          (head=(ancestor ?x ?y) body=(goals (parent ?x ?z) (ancestor ?z ?y) :done))))
  (solve (ancestor :abe ?who) db))
# => (sols (who=:bob) (who=:carl))

solve returns every solution — (ancestor ?a ?b) yields all three ancestor
pairs — and the bare symbol sols when there are none. Resolution is
depth-first with backtracking driven by iterating the clauses; each clause
invocation is freshened with a tag taken from its recursion path (symbol
builds names like ?x_3_2 at runtime), and term-equal compares terms
structurally without reducing them, so (1 + 2) is data rather than 3.

What the code exercises: hold= on def parameters passes a term into a
function unreduced; ~(keyword (name v))=… is a computed map key; and the
sentinels (:done, sols, (vs :done))
mark the end of the search. One sharp edge: a bound variable must
not share its name with the head of its own value. (let (db=db) db) is fine —
replacing db by itself is a fixed point and yields db — but a non-trivial
value such as (let (db=(db 1)) db) re-resolves its head db to the value again
until the recursion limit, hence the clauses marker above.

What worked well. The whole suite now runs: persistent collections with
with/wout/join, map/filter/reduce/for, frequencies, and
partition-by cover Tier 1; operator-anchored rules, guards, lower, loop/recur
and replacement-rule lambdas cover Tier 2; the RETE engine (logic-set, assert/retract/

the concurrent counter; eval, rewriting, get-indexed grids, the infix-aware

Fixed while doing this. A core engine bug: user rules matched the raw form,
so a scope-bound symbol inside it was not resolved before matching (a rule body’s
(d f x) matched the wrong rule). The fix is a general scope protocol — each
binding form (let/loop/for/a replacement rule) declares its binders, and the reducer
resolves scope bindings before matching while leaving binding positions alone.
Two smaller additions came out of the Prolog engine: (symbol x) builds a symbol
from a string at runtime (needed for variable freshening), and equal? was
renamed eq?.

Remaining gaps.

Search on top of constraint propagation (#15) — expressible, not written.

Hygiene — a bound name that also heads its own value expands without end
(see the note under #25); data is safest with names distinct from variables.

This document summarizes the architectural strategy for managing ephemeral, host-level execution resources (such as promises, tasks, and sockets) as extern types within Air, and how they interact with the persistence layer (AirDB.jl).

Extern Types: Low-level system resources and concurrency primitives are implemented as specialized Julia types managed directly by the host language’s garbage collector (GC).

First-Class In-Memory Representation: In-memory Air forms can seamlessly contain live Julia object references as leaf nodes, allowing operations like (await p) to execute with native performance.

Extensibility: Extern types are defined statically at startup via user-defined Julia methods implementing the Air extern protocol.

Because active sockets and in-flight tasks cannot be serialized as raw pointers to PostgreSQL, extern objects participate in a clean serialization protocol mapped to structured S-expressions in JSONB.

Serialized Form Shape:(extern :type payload)

Deserialization: When loaded from AirDB.jl, the runtime dispatches the form back through the registered startup extern methods to reconstruct the appropriate state or wrapper.

To avoid complex, race-prone asynchronous database row-mutations for in-flight tasks:

Ephemeral Resource Rule: Active, unresolved execution primitives are treated strictly as runtime execution state rather than permanent domain state.

The Tombstone Approach: When an active or pending extern object (such as an unfulfilled promise) hits the database serializer during a write/commit, it is immediately converted into an inert, serializable tombstone:(extern :promise :abandoned)

Behavior on Recovery: If application code encounters an expired or abandoned extern tombstone post-recovery, it fails cleanly with a structured runtime error (e.g., :extern-expired) rather than hanging indefinitely.

The concurrency primitives that can be persisted are not externs at all: they
are AirDB reference forms with their own serializations, and AirLang exposes one
constructor per kind.

Actors. (send a fn) calls fn with the current value and persists the
result; inside a transaction the send is deferred to commit, and (sync)
flushes. The send captures the caller’s lexical names like a task (inner
binders shadow) and keeps the sender’s namespace layers and val bindings.
(reset! a value) replaces the value directly. Every update is
written to form_actor_current (plus form_actor_history when history is
on, fixed at creation).

Promises. (deliver p v) fills a promise once; (get p)/(await p)
read it (blocking outside a transaction, raising inside one unless it is
already delivered) and (ready? p) tests it. A promise stores a row and
always encodes as a link, whether it is pending or delivered, so a reader
waits on the same promise rather than on a copy of its value.

Delays. The registration registry (register_delay) is keyed by a type
name, and the loader sees only the serialized form. AirLang registers :air
once at startup; its serialization is a VolatileForm cell. The cell first
holds a tagged thunk — the substituted body plus the captured namespace path,
active using layers, val bindings, @ root, and .env — and is replaced
by the computed value on the first force. That is what makes the cache durable:
a fresh process that opens the database finds the value already computed and
never runs the body. The Env the force runs in is installed task-locally for
the dynamic extent of the call (the loader has no environment argument), and
the body runs as the user who forces it, like a stored def. A value the
database cannot hold, or a user without write access, is simply not cached;
the delay still yields the value. Printing and encoding never force a delay,
and a body that forces its own delay raises a catchable
(error :internal "a delay cannot force itself").

Most externs wrap a live resource and must die with the process. bytes is the
opposite: an opaque, immutable octet string that persists, compares by
content, and prints opaquely.(bytes "hello")            ; from a string's bytes
(bytes-of (104 105))       ; from a sequence of integers
(bytes-length b)           ; the octet count
(bytes-string b)           ; the raw octets as a string
(bytes-index b 1)          ; one octet as an integer (1-based)
(bytes-slice b 2 3)        ; a sub-range, as bytes
(bytes? x)

Because it is immutable and its equality is structural, two bytes values with
the same contents are the same air value: eq? and hash agree, so it works as
a memo key and in a keyed table. Its registration supplies serialize
(write(io, data)), deserialize (read(io)), equal, and hash to
register_extern, so a database stores and reloads the raw octets. It does
not round-trip through to-json/from-json: those write an unnamed extern
as an opaque marker, and reading it back yields a DeadExtern. Move a payload
through a database or an SFTP transfer instead. Printing is opaque —
#<bytes 1048576> — so a file-sized payload never floods a result or a log.

It is the value a transferred file becomes and the value a local file is read
back from: the SSH subsystem (

SSH access) turns a remote path into a
namespace path and a file into a bytes val.

A 

table is the second immutable, content-valued extern. It holds
persistent columns (FormSeq views over Air’s PVectors), an ordered name
list, a per-column _ColumnMeta (type and NA marker), a row count, and an
optional index dictionary. The registration supplies serialize, deserialize,
equal, and hash, so a committed table reloads with its schema and NA markers
intact, and eq?/hash agree on tables whose columns are in a different order
or whose cells are equivalent.

Like bytes, a table is stored faithfully in a database but does not survive
to-json/from-json text; for interchange use CSV/TSV or a database.

Status of §3. The tombstone scheme is not what the runtime does today: an
unnamed extern is written without an id and reads back as a DeadExtern that
prints #<extern :type (expired)> and raises (error :extern-expired :type)
when touched. A task returns a database PromiseForm, so its promise
survives a round trip (as a link until delivered); the running task itself is a
process item and cannot be serialized, so a promise whose task never delivered
is simply never delivered.

air reads and writes six text formats — JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV, TSV, and
.env — as plain air data. An object or table becomes a map form, an array
a sequence form, and a scalar a scalar; CSV and TSV decode to a


table and encode from one. Nothing else becomes an extern type,
and nothing in a file is ever executed. Decoding is therefore safe: a YAML file
cannot construct an object or call a function, however its tags are written.(decode "{\"a\": [1, 2], \"b\": null}" format=:json)   # => (a=(1 2) b=naught)
(encode (a=(1 2) b=naught) format=:json)               # => "{\"a\":[1,2],\"b\":null}"

form

meaning

parse text (a string or bytes) into a form

(encode v format=:json)

encode a form as text

(read-data path)

read a file, inferring the format from its name

(read-data path format=:yaml)

read a file in an explicit format

(write-data path v)

encode v and write it to a file

(write-data path v format=:toml)

write in an explicit format

format accepts a keyword, a symbol, or a string, and yml and dotenv are
aliases of yaml and env. The default for decode and encode is :json.
read-data and write-data infer the format from the extension (.json,
.yaml, .yml, .toml, .csv, .tsv, or the file name .env) and raise
when they cannot.(read-data "config.toml")               # => (server=(host="localhost" port=8080))
(write-data "out.yaml" (a=1 b=(1 2)))   # writes "a: 1\nb:\n  - 1\n  - 2\n"

Like write-file, write-data defers the write to the transaction commit, so a
transaction that aborts writes nothing.

The path helpers are gated by the filesystem permission on .air.sys, and
a fresh instance grants it only to air: read-data and write-data refuse
any other identity with (:permission-denied :filesystem :read-data) until
air runs (chmod! .air.sys filesystem=(:alice)). Startup code and libraries
(which run as air) use them freely; a shared configuration value reaches a
user through a namespace or a database, not through a host path. decode and
encode touch no file — they read a string or a bytes value — and need no
permission. See 

users, homes, and permissions.

The formats differ in what they can express; the mapping to forms is the same.

object / table / mapping

Because an empty object and an empty array both become naught, the round trip
is lossy for empty containers: {"a": {}} and {"a": []} both encode as
(a=naught), which writes back as {"a": null}. A list holding empties keeps
its length — [{}, []] is (naught naught) — but each element is null.

A map key is normalized to its text, so {1: "x"} and {"1": "x"} name the
same air key. In a form the key is the air keyword spelling, which is the text
with a leading :; the printer drops that colon, so keys read naturally. Two
keys that normalize alike are a duplicate and raise rather than silently
overwriting.

A value is plain data if it is a scalar, a string, a keyword or symbol (which
encode as their text), a sequence of plain data, or a map of plain data. A
container that mixes sequence elements and map entries ((f a=1)) has no
representation in any format and raises. So does an extern, a mutable, a
reference form, a rational, or a complex number. Map keys are emitted in sorted
order in every format, so encoding is deterministic.

A 

table is the one extern with a plain-data shape: it encodes as
an array of its row maps, [{"a":1,"b":"x"},{"a":2,"b":"y"}]. Decoding that
returns the row maps, not a table — the schema is not carried by JSON or YAML —
so use CSV/TSV when a table needs to round-trip.(encode (name="x" count=1) format=:json)     # => "{\"count\":1,\"name\":\"x\"}"
(encode (1 a=2) format=:json)                # a map and a sequence in one form: error
(encode (/ 1 3) format=:json)                # a rational has no data representation: error

The reader is strict RFC 8259: objects, arrays, strings with the standard
escapes and \u surrogate pairs, true/false/null, and numbers with no
leading zero, trailing decimal point, or stray text. A duplicate key, an
unpaired surrogate, a truncated document, or trailing garbage is an error.

An integer that fits Int64 decodes as an Int64, a larger one as a BigInt,
and a number with a fraction or exponent as a Float64. Encoding rejects a
non-finite float (inf, -inf, nan), because JSON has no spelling for one.(decode "[1, 2.5, true, null, \"x\\n\"]")       # => (1 2.5 true naught "x\n")
(decode "9223372036854775808")                  # a BigInt
(encode naught format=:json)                    # => "null"

The YAML reader covers the practical subset a configuration file uses and is
safe by construction:

block mappings and sequences (a: 1, - 1), with sequences permitted at the
indentation of their parent key;

flow mappings and sequences ({a: 1}, [1, 2]), which may span lines;

plain, single-quoted, and double-quoted scalars, with '' doubling and the
Julia-style escapes (\n, \t, \x, \u, \U, \N, \_, \L, \P);

block scalars — literal | and folded >, with the strip (-), clip, and
keep (+) chomping modes and explicit indentation indicators;

comments, anchors and aliases (&name / *name), the << merge key, and
multi-document streams (--- / ...);

the core-schema resolution of plain scalars.

In the core schema a plain ~/null is naught, true/false are booleans,
decimal, 0x, and 0o integers are integers, and .inf/.nan are floats.
Everything else — including yes/no/on/off (which YAML 1.1 treats as
booleans) and bare dates — stays a string, as YAML 1.2 says.(decode "a: [1, 2]\nb:\n  c: |\n    x\n    y\n" format=:yaml)
# => (a=(1 2) b=(c="x\ny\n"))
(decode "yes: 2026-10-30\n" format=:yaml)     # => (yes="2026-10-30")

Tags are never constructed. The core tags (!!str, !!int, !!float,
!!bool, !!null, !!map, !!seq) are understood and apply their type; any
other tag — !!python/object, !custom, a %TAG directive — is an error.
That is the whole safety property: a YAML file from an untrusted source can only
produce data.

The reader bounds its work: nesting deeper than 256 levels, more than one
million nodes (including the size an alias expands to), a tab in indentation, or
an unknown alias is an error. Anchors are expanded when an alias is read, so an
“alias bomb” fails at the node limit instead of exhausting memory.

A stream with more than one document needs documents=true, which returns them
as a sequence; an empty or comment-only stream is naught. The encoder writes
block style with sorted keys, and a multi-document stream cannot be encoded
(encode each document and join them yourself).(decode "---\na: 1\n---\nb: 2\n" format=:yaml documents=true)   # => ((a=1) (b=2))
(decode "a: !!int \"5\"\n" format=:yaml)                       # => (a=5)
(decode "a: !!python/object x\n" format=:yaml)                 # error: unsupported tag

TOML maps onto forms directly: a table is a map form, an array a sequence form,
and an inline table a nested map. The document itself must be a table, so the
top level of a decoded TOML file is always a map form (an empty document is
naught). Tables encode after the scalar entries, as [section] headers; an
array is written inline, with a map element as an inline table.

TOML has no null, so a naught value cannot be encoded; only the empty
document is naught.(decode "port = 8080\n[db]\nhost = \"x\"\n" format=:toml)
# => (db=(host="x") port=8080)
(encode (port=8080 db=(host="x")) format=:toml)
# => "port = 8080\n\n[db]\nhost = \"x\"\n"
(encode (a=naught) format=:toml)             # error: TOML has no null

TOML integers are 64-bit, so a BigInt outside that range raises. A float is
written as nan, inf, -inf, or a decimal that always keeps a fractional
part.

TOML has native dates, times, and datetimes, which have no counterpart among
air’s values. They decode as marker forms that carry the literal text:(decode "d = 2026-10-30\nt = 12:30:00\nk = 2026-10-30T12:30:00\n" format=:toml)
# => (d=(toml-date "2026-10-30") k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00")
#     t=(toml-time "12:30:00"))

The markers are ordinary air data — a two-element form headed toml-date,
toml-time, or toml-datetime. Encoding one writes its text unquoted when the
text is a valid literal of that kind and raises otherwise, so a marker never
silently becomes a string. Any other form of the same shape is an ordinary map.

An offset date-time keeps its offset exactly as written, including a
trailing Z:(decode "k = 2026-10-30T12:30:00-08:00\n" format=:toml)
# => (k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00-08:00"))
(decode "k = 2026-10-30T12:30:00Z\n" format=:toml)
# => (k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00Z"))

The standard library’s parser rejects ±hh:mm and drops Z, so the reader
protects each bare offset date-time before parsing and restores the marker
afterward; a date-time inside a string or a comment stays string data.

A decode produces a 

table; an encode accepts a table or a
non-empty sequence of row maps. The parser is a dependency-free RFC 4180 state
machine over UTF-8 text, and the column and row delimiters are options.

option

decode

encode

absent: infer; true: the first record names the columns; false: :col1…:colN; (names…): explicit names, no header consumed

true (default) writes the names; false omits them; (names…) writes explicit labels

column-delimiter

one-character string; default , (\t for tsv)

same

string; default LF, accepting CRLF/LF/CR; when given, only that string ends a record and CR/LF are data

same; default \n

per-column output coercion

per-column missing marker

rejected(decode "name,age\nBob,51\nSue,42" format=:csv)     # => #table(2×2: name, age)
(schema (decode "name,age\nBob,51\nSue,42" format=:csv))
# => (age=(na=NA type=:int) name=(na=NA type=:string))
(decode "1,2\n3,4" format=:csv)                     # => #table(2×2: col1, col2)
(encode (table a=(1 2) b=("x" "y")) format=:csv)    # => "a,b\n1,x\n2,y\n"
(encode ((a=1 b="x") (a=2 b="y")) format=:csv)      # the same text

Header inference. When header is absent, the first record is a header iff
no field in it is a plain number: a canonical integer spelling (no leading
zeros), or a finite Float64 (a fraction or exponent). Empty fields, NA, and
NaN do not count, so an all-string first row is a header and a row with any
number is data. This is a heuristic: a headerless all-string file loses its
first row, and a header row containing a numeric-looking field is treated as
data — pass header= whenever either is possible. header=false always names
the columns :col1…:colN, and header=("x" "y") names them explicitly
without consuming a record.

Parsing. A quote opens a quoted field only at its start; inside it a
doubled "" is a literal quote and every delimiter and newline is data. A quote
inside an unquoted field, text after a closing quote, or an unterminated field
raises, as does a record whose width differs from the header’s. CRLF, LF, and CR
all end a default-delimited record and a trailing terminator adds no row, so an
empty text is a 0-row table. Errors name the record number.

Types and NA. Fields are inferred with canonical rules: :int only for an
optional - and digits with no leading zero (so 007 stays a string), :float
only for a finite parse that is not an integer (so 1e3 is a float), :bool
only for true/false, and otherwise :string. types= overrides the
inference; declaring :string, :symbol, or :keyword keeps the field’s text,
while :int, :float, :number, and :bool parse it. An empty field is the
column’s NA, and the text NA or NaN is missing unless the column declares a
different marker with na=. A missing cell writes back as an empty field.(schema (decode "a,b\n1,2.5" format=:csv))
# => (a=(na=NA type=:int) b=(na=NaN type=:float))
(get (decode "a\n007\n1e3\ntrue\nNA" format=:csv) :a)
# => ("007" 1000.0 true NA)
(decode "n,a\nBob,1\nSue,2" format=:csv index=:n)   # an indexed table
(encode (table a=(1 NA) b=(NaN 2.0)) format=:csv)   # => "a,b\n1,\n,2.0\n"
(encode (table a=(1 2)) format=:csv columns=(:a) header=false)   # => "1\n2\n"

TSV is not the IANA backslash convention. It is RFC 4180 quoting with a tab
column delimiter: a tab, a newline, or a " inside a field is quoted by doubling
the quotes, exactly as for CSV.

What is lost. CSV carries no types of its own: a symbol or keyword decodes as
a string unless types= says otherwise, a "007" field stays a string, and a
naught cell cannot be spelled (declare an na= and use it, or encode a
different format). Encoding a naught cell, a container cell, or a non-finite
float that is not the column’s NA raises.

A .env file is a flat mapping of variable names to text. Decoding accepts
comments, blank lines, an export  prefix, and empty, single-quoted,
double-quoted, and bare values; an unquoted # after whitespace starts a
comment, and \n, \t, \\, \", and \' are recognized in double quotes.
A name must be a letter or _ followed by letters, digits, _, ., or -.
Duplicate names and a line that is not name=value raise.

Every value is a string — .env has no numbers, booleans, or nulls — so
A=1 decodes as (A="1"). Encoding requires a map at the top level whose
values are scalars; a naught value writes an empty value, and a value needing
quotes is double-quoted.(decode "export A=1\nB=\"x y\"\n" format=:env)     # => (A="1" B="x y")
(encode (B="x y" A="1") format=:env)               # => "A=1\nB=\"x y\"\n"
(encode (a=(1 2)) format=:env)                     # error: .env values are strings

Note that .env keys are conventionally uppercase, but air does not enforce or
change case: (A="1") writes A=1 and (a="1") writes a=1.

Databases describes AirDB’s to-json and from-json, which
also produce text. They are a serialization codec: a volatile becomes a
"@uuid" link, a non-finite float is the marked string "#inf", and a cycle is
legal. encode/decode are a data codec: every value is written out
literally, links are not followed, and a non-finite float or a cyclic value is
an error. Use to-json to move air values between databases and encode to
exchange plain data with another program.

JSON nesting is bounded at 512 levels; YAML at 256, with a one-million-node
total.

JSON, YAML, TOML, and .env round-trip plain, non-empty data exactly under
eq?; decode(encode(x)) is not x for an empty container, which becomes
naught, or for a TOML date marker written to another format, which becomes a
map or a string. A table round-trips through CSV/TSV with its schema, but a
symbol, keyword, or "007" field returns as a string unless types= names
the column’s type.

There is no spreadsheet reader (.xlsx and friends) yet; CSV and TSV are
covered above.

cd AirLang.jl
julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'

Pkg.instantiate() resolves the path dependencies and downloads the registered
ones (Air uses DataStructures; AirDB uses LibPQ). Precompiling happens on
first use:julia --project=. -e 'using AirLang'

bin/air is the command line. With no arguments it starts a read-eval-print
loop; -e evaluates one chunk of code; any other argument is a file to load:./bin/air                              # the REPL
./bin/air -e '(+ 1 2)'                 # => 3
./bin/air -e 'using AirLang; (println "hi")'
./bin/air program.air                  # load a file

The -e chunks and files in one invocation share an environment, so definitions
made by an earlier -e are visible to a later one. The REPL reads a form across
lines while the reader reports an unterminated form, string, or block comment
(with a ...>  continuation prompt) and sets AIR_HISTORY to a file that each
complete input is appended to, for use with external line editors such as
rlwrap.

From Julia, the same entry points are available as functions:using AirLang, AirDB

env = Env(db = MemoryDatabase())          # a private in-memory database
air_eval(env, read_air("(+ 1 2)"))        # => 3
air_string(air_eval(env, read_air("(let (x=2) (* x 3))")))   # => "6"

air_eval, read_air, air_string, air_pretty_string, air_repl,
open_airdb!, and close_airdb! are exported. Env carries the process
database; see 

Databases.

lib/ in this repository is the first entry of AIR_LIBPATH, the
:-separated (Windows: ;) list of directories air searches when a library is
first needed; the default is <repo>/lib followed by ~/.air/lib. A library is
a directory holding an init.air:lib/

(.lib.math.twice 4)          # the loaded namespace is reachable too

The repository ships a Dockerfile and a docker-compose.yml. The image is a

Or use the compose file, which names the same contexts and also starts a

bin/air-docker is a thin wrapper that runs the image with the same command

./bin/air-docker program.air

Inside the container the library path is /air/lib (the mount) and Julia’s

The test suite needs only the default in-memory database; the PostgreSQL tests

AIRLANG_TEST_PG_URL="postgresql://air:air@localhost/air" \
    julia --project=. test/runtests.jl

julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test()' is the same suite under Pkg’s
isolation. The docker-compose.yml sidecar provides a PostgreSQL server with
user, password, and database air:docker compose up -d postgres

Air is a Clojure- and Mathematica-inspired scripting language that runs on
Julia. It is implemented by AirLang.jl, which builds on two libraries:

Air.jl — Clojure-like immutable
data structures and a software transactional memory (STM); and

AirDB.jl — a persistence layer
that stores Air forms in PostgreSQL jsonb tables in transaction order.

Air’s two rule systems make it a natural interface to a reasoning and rules
system: one evaluates code by term rewriting (def, replace, lambdas), and
the other derives and maintains facts in a logic set (assert, rule,
query). Everything — code, data, rules, and errors — is the same kind of
immutable, inspectable form.

The short version

Air is a Lisp whose values are JSON-like forms, whose functions are rewrite
rules, whose namespaces are multi-user logic sets persisted in PostgreSQL, and
whose errors are matched structurally rather than by class.

(+ 1 2)                             # => 3
(let (x=2 y=3) (* x y))             # => 6
(thread (f (1 2 3)))                # => ((f 1) (f 2) (f 3))
(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x) depth=1)   # => (1 2)

Definitions are patterns, and the body is a replacement:(def (fact ?n)
  (if (< n 2) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1)))))

(fact 5)                            # => 120

Facts and rules live in a namespace, which is implicitly a logic set:(namespace .app)
(assert .app (depends :app :lib1))
(assert .app (rule (depends ?x ?y) :> (needs ?x ?y)))

(facts .app)                        # => (' (depends :app :lib1) (needs :app :lib1))
(query .app (needs ?x ?y))          # => ((x=:app y=:lib1))
