(load-air path…) evaluates every form in every named file, in order. It reads
and parses every file before evaluating any form, then evaluates inside
one transaction, so a parse error or a runtime error leaves nothing behind. It
returns the last value. A relative path resolves against the directory of the
file that contains the load-air call (the process working directory at top
level), not against the caller’s current directory:(load-air "util.air")   ; next to the loading file (or the cwd at top level)

The air command line uses the same loader: air file.air and air -e '…'.
The system namespace exposes the same functions as .air.sys.load-air,
.air.sys.read-file, and so on.

A library is a directory whose name is a valid name segment and that
contains an init.air. AIR_LIBPATH is a :-separated list of search
directories (; on Windows), read when a library is first needed; the default
is <repo>/lib and ~/.air/lib, and the first directory with a matching
<name>/init.air wins. A library loads lazily — when .lib.<name> is first
addressed, or when a bare using/import spec names it:(using math (twice 4))       ; loads <libpath>/math/init.air if needed
(.lib.math.twice 4)          ; same

init.air runs as air, with .lib.<name> as the current namespace and the
library directory as the loading directory, in one transaction under a
per-library lock. A failed load registers nothing ((.lib.bad …) raises the
error the file raised; .lib has no bad entry afterwards). A recursive
reference to a library already loading is declined rather than deadlocking.

A namespace is an ordered collection of def and val definitions addressed by
a dotted path. . alone is the global namespace root; .air is the core
namespace, holding every builtin, operator, standard-library name, and constant
(pi, e, tau, inf, nan). A leading-dot atom is a path:
.util.algebra.square reads as (get . :util :algebra :square), so the whole
namespace tree is ordinary . access over nested namespace values. A bare name
in a namespace form is a root-level name, so (namespace util …) is
(namespace .util …).

The root holds the process’s system namespaces:

path

contents

.air

the generated core namespace: builtins, operators, constants (owned by air, world r-x)

.air.sys

the system functions: load-air, read-file, write-file, read-data, write-data, open-airdb, close-airdb

.sys

system state; readable only by air

.sys.user.<name>

a system user’s record and home

.lib

the library cache (owned by air, world r-x)

.main

air’s startup namespace

.env

a val holding the task’s environment mapping

Every entry in a namespace is itself a volatile with its own metadata — owner,
ACL, provenance, and an optional anchor — so two users may own different
definitions in one namespace, and an import is an explicit, inspectable entry
rather than a transient lookup. Metadata is visible to anyone who can reach an
entry; the body is gated by its read permission (see 

Users, homes, and
permissions).(namespace .util
  (def (twice ?x) (* x 2))
  (val answer 42))
(.util.twice 4)      # => 8
(.util.answer)       # => 42

def and val inside a namespace block append to that namespace, and a
subnamespace is created automatically: (namespace .util.algebra (…)) registers
algebra inside .util (creating any missing ancestors). A namespace block is
a transaction — if a body form fails, everything the block defined rolls back. A
subnamespace may never shadow a definition of the same name, in either order, and
neither may a definition shadow a subnamespace.

Definitions added later are matched first, so a reload or override wins:(namespace .util (def (twice ?x) (* x 2)))
(namespace .util (def (twice ?x) (+ x x)))
(.util.twice 4)      # => 8, from the later definition

A zero-argument call applies a definition too: (.util.f) calls f, matching
either (def (f) …) or a scalar (def f …).

hierarchy.lvl2: Roots, homes, and the current namespace
Roots, homes, and the current namespace

records.content:
Three addresses are resolved by the running task rather than by fixed paths:

$ — the current user’s home namespace: .sys.user.<u>.home for a system
user, @.user.<u>.home for a database user. It is a capability held directly
by the task, so a user works in their home without being able to read .sys
(or the user records enclosing it).

@ — the root namespace of the database the task is attached to. An
unattached user sees @ as . (the air root).

The current namespace — task-local: $ for a created user, .main for
air at boot. A top-level def/val is written there, so it is durable: an
entry in a namespace rather than a process-global rule. (namespace path body…) replaces the current namespace for body and does not layer the
caller’s definitions, which is what makes (namespace .air …) pristine;
using=(ns…) activates namespaces for the body without nesting it.

$ and @ are ordinary symbols: a lexically bound name shadows them and let
may rebind them ((let ($=8) $) → 8), so bind them as data, not as code.

A .-atom address is not the only spelling a namespace-taking form accepts.
(get $ :config) and a leading-. path name the same namespace, and every form
that resolves an address — namespace, using, use, import, unuse,
clear, open-airdb, and the logic-set targets — accepts either, so
(namespace $.config.ssh (val authorized-keys ("…"))) writes
.sys.user.<u>.home.config.ssh. The resolver checks a bound name first: when
the body has bound $ (or @) lexically, the form is evaluated normally and
the binding wins, exactly as it does for a bare $.

The task’s identity, current namespace, database root, and .env mapping
travel with spawned tasks, so a task sees the same roots (see


Tasks).

(using spec… body…) activates one namespace, or a list of them, for body:
the namespace’s rules are searched (below body’s own definitions and above the
global store) and its vals become resolvable names. using copies nothing; it
is context for the body. A spec is a namespace address with optional only=,
except=, and as= options, written either as keyword pairs in the spec’s
sequence or in its map:(using .util (twice 4))
(using (.util :only (twice answer)) (twice 4))
(using (.util :except (answer)) (twice 4))
(using ((.util :only (twice)) (.util.algebra :as alg)) (get alg :square))

Later specs have priority over earlier ones. as= binds the namespace value
itself to a name (it does not add a dot path).

Inside a namespace block, (use spec…) and (import spec…) materialize
the selected names as entries of the current namespace. use keeps them private
(they compile into the namespace’s rules but are absent from its map); import
also exports them in the map. What is stored depends on what the importer may do
with the source entry:

source entry

stored entry

readable def

a copy, owned by the target namespace’s owner, carrying the source’s ACL

readable val

an entry that shares the source’s Var, so a rebinding of the source is visible

execute-only, a proxy, or anchor=true

a proxy storing (source path, name); it applies the source lazily with the source entry’s owner and ACL

subnamespace

a link entry, resolved through the source namespace

Every imported entry records source=<namespace> in its metadata. Re-importing
a name replaces the previous entry from that source, so an import is how a
namespace is refreshed. A proxy keeps an execute-only body hidden; a missing
source raises (error :proxy-unresolved path) at call time. (chmod! entry anchor=true) marks an entry so that it is always imported as a proxy, even when
it is readable.(namespace .algebra
  (use .util)                        ; may call (twice 2) inside this namespace
  (import (.util :only (answer)))    ; `answer` becomes part of `.algebra`
  (def (quad ?x) (* (twice (twice x)) 2)))
(algebra.quad 3)                     # => 24
(get . :algebra :answer)             # => 42

Removal:

(clear sym) removes the current block’s entries that define or export sym,
including imported copies; (clear :all) removes every definition and import
(local subnamespaces stay).

(unuse ns) removes the block’s entries imported from ns; (unuse ns name…) removes just those names (provenance is the entry’s source=).

(del sym) is an alias of clear. Outside a namespace block, clear targets
the process-global rule store and never removes a builtin, operator, or core
constant.

(val pattern form…) is like def, but form is evaluated once at definition
time and the pattern is installed as a value rather than a function — it cannot
be called. Each val is backed by an Air Var, so its value is thread-local:
a bind shadows it in the current task only and restores the previous value when
its body finishes. bind names values by the name its namespace context matches,
so it rebinds exactly the val that a bare reference would see:(val x 10)
(bind (x=99) x)                             # => 99
x                                           # => 10
(using .util (bind (answer=1) (twice 1)))   # => 3

The binding form is evaluated before it is used, so its values are ordinary
expressions ((bind (x=(x + 1)) x) → 11). Binding a name that is not a val in
the current context is an error. bind is dynamic, not lexical: it affects calls
into rules and namespace functions made within its body.

(bindings) evaluates to a mapping of the current task’s overrides — the vals
whose value differs from its definition value — and that mapping can be
reinstalled with bind:(bind (x=1 y=2) (bindings))     # => (x=1 y=2)
(bind (x=5) (bind (bindings) x))   # => 5

(task form…) holds its arguments and evaluates them on a separate task,
returning a database-backed promise immediately. (await p) blocks until
the task finishes and returns the value of the final form, or rethrows the
task’s error; (get p) and (ready? p) read the same promise. A task captures
its enclosing lexical scope (like a closure), keeps the namespace context active
at the point it was created, and inherits the current task’s val bindings:(val x 10)
(bind (x=100) (await (task (+ x 1))))   # => 101

The spawned task receives a copy of the bindings, so a later bind in the parent
does not change what the task sees. A task is a process item: its promise lives
in the current namespace’s database, but the running task itself is not
serialized, so a promise whose task never delivered (because the process
stopped) is simply never delivered.

Three reference forms are backed by live objects and by the database, so they
survive a serialization round trip.

(delay body…) computes its body lazily and at most once. (get d), (get d 0),
and any get path that walks through d force it; a delay vanishes on the
path exactly as a mutable does. Free lexical names are substituted into the body
like a task’s, and the namespace context active at creation — the current
namespace, its active using layers, the thread-local val bindings, @, and
.env — is saved with it, so the body runs correctly later, even after the
database is reopened. The first force stores the value in the delay’s database
cell and every later force returns it without running the body again:(val counter (mut 0))
(val d (delay (set! counter (+ (get counter) 1))))
(get d)        # => 1
(get d)        # => 1 (the body does not run again)
(get counter)  # => 1

A delay is immutable and never forces on printing or serialization. The body
runs as the user who forces it (like a stored def), and a body that forces its
own delay raises a catchable error rather than recursing.

(actor value history=true) is a sequential worker whose value is persisted on
every update. (send a fn) sends the function fn (which receives the current
value and returns the new one) and (reset! a value) replaces the value
directly; both are deferred to commit inside a transaction, and (sync) flushes
a pending send. The send closes over the caller’s lexical scope the way a task
does: a loop/for binding or rule parameter used inside fn is substituted
with its value, and the namespace context active at the call (its using
layers and val bindings) is kept, so a rule name or a val still resolves.
A name bound by the function’s own pattern shadows the captured one, so
(for (x …) (send a (?x -> …))) uses the parameter, not the loop’s x.
(actor? x) tests one.

(promise) is a single-assignment value in the current namespace’s database.
(deliver p v) fills it (once), (get p)/(await p) read it — blocking until
it is delivered, except inside a transaction, which raises instead — and
(ready? p) tests it. A promise serializes as a link ("~uuid") whether it is
pending or delivered, and stores a row either way, so a reader of the stored
form waits on the same promise rather than on a copy of its value. task
returns such a promise; deliver and await also accept an ephemeral promise
extern.

A number in air is one of the eight leaves AirDB stores and serializes:

leaf

written

example

Int64

digits that fit the machine word

42

BigInt

any other integer

123456789012345678901234567890

Float64

a decimal point, an exponent, or Inf/NaN

1.5, 1e9, -Inf

BigFloat

big"…"

big"1.5"

Rational{Int64}

n//d

1//3

Rational{BigInt}

n//d with a large part

123456789012345678901234567890//7

ComplexF64

a+bi with no space

4.4+2.0i, 2i

Complex{BigFloat}

big"…"i, or (complex re im)

big"2.0"i

These are exactly AirDB’s FormLeaf types, so a number written in air, read
from a database, or decoded from JSON is the same Julia value.

Integers are read as Int64 when they fit and as BigInt otherwise; an
integer-shaped token never silently becomes a float. A // with no spaces
around it is a rational literal, and the sign is normalized onto the numerator
(1//-3 reads as -1//3). big"…" parses a BigFloat at the ambient
precision, and the usual prefixed-literal spellings work anywhere a form may
appear (x=big"1.5", 'big"1.5").

Inf, -Inf, and NaN are the spellings the printer emits, and they read
back as the Float64 values they name. The constants inf and nan are also
available as bare symbols.

A complex value prints as one atom with no space around the sign —
4.4+2.0i, not 4.4 + 2.0i — so a printed form re-reads as the same value at
any depth. A complex value whose real part is zero still prints its zero
(0.0+2.0i), and a Complex{BigFloat} prints as (complex big"re" big"im")
because a bare re+imi atom could not be read back as the same type.

Every number prints in a spelling the reader accepts and that denotes the same
value, at any depth:1//3                      # => 1//3
big"1.5"                  # => big"1.5"
(f 4.4+2.0i)              # => (f 4.4+2.0i)

A BigFloat whose precision is the ambient precision(BigFloat) prints as
big"…". Any other precision prints with the annotation, because big"…"
would silently re-read at the ambient precision instead:(bigfloat "1.5" precision=512)

Three constructors build the values the reader cannot spell directly:

(rational n d) — the exact rational n/d; a zero denominator raises.

(complex re im) — the complex value with those parts; ComplexF64 when
both parts are exactly Float64, Complex{BigFloat} otherwise.

(bigfloat "…" precision=n) — a BigFloat parsed at n bits (default: the
ambient precision).

Arithmetic is Julia’s, and air adds no promotion rules of its own. Both
operands must be numbers and the result is canonicalized to a leaf; a value
that is not a number leaves the form symbolic ((x + 1)).

/ always divides in floating point: (/ 1 2) is 0.5, and / of two
rationals stays exact ((/ 1//2 2) is 1//4).

// is the exact rational constructor, as in Julia: (7 // 2) is
7//2, and a zero denominator raises. Integer division is the div verb:
(div 7 2) is 3, and (div -7 2) is -3 (it truncates toward zero).

mod keeps Julia’s meaning (the result has the sign of the divisor), and
(mod 7//2 1) is 1//2.

Exact inputs give exact results: (+ 1//3 1//6) is 1//2, and an operation
with a BigInt operand stays a BigInt without overflow
((* 1267650600228229401496703205376 2) is 2535301200456458802993406410752).

Int64 arithmetic wraps, as in Julia: (^ 2 100) is 0. Write a literal
that does not fit an Int64, or a rational, to keep the result exact.

The math verbs (abs, sqrt, floor, round, sin, …) are Julia functions
too, so they follow the type of their argument: (floor 7//2) is 3//1, and
(sqrt -1) is an error rather than a complex value.

number? is true for any of the eight leaves. int? and integer? are true
for Int64 and BigInt, float? for Float64 and BigFloat, and
complex? for the two complex types. A rational is a number but not an
integer, even when it is whole ((int? 1//1) is false). zero?, even?,
odd?, positive?, negative?, nan?, and infinite? accept whatever
Julia accepts for their type.

The three relations in 

the data model
treat numbers as follows:

eq? is AirDB’s isequiv: the same type and the same value. (eq? 1 1.0),
(eq? 1 1//1), and (eq? 1 big"1.0") are all false. A signed zero is one
value ((eq? -0.0 0.0) is true) and NaN is equivalent to itself.

== is content equality, which is AirDB’s == on forms. It is
numeric-friendly, so (== 1 1.0) is true and (== -0.0 0.0) is true; a
NaN is equal to nothing, as in Julia.

(hash x) follows eq?, so equivalent numbers hash alike and 1 and
1.0, which are not equivalent, need not.

(compare a b) and the ordering operators order two Real values numerically.
A complex value has no order, so an ordering comparison that involves one stays
symbolic — (< 1 2.0+1.0i) — while compare falls back to the printed
spelling so that its order stays total.

AirDB’s codec carries every leaf. An integer too large for Int64 is the
string "#big:…", a rational "#rat:n/d" or "#bigrat:n/d", a big float
"#bigfloat:<bits>:…", and a non-finite float "#inf", "#-inf", or
"#nan". from-json returns the same value to-json was given, including the
precision of a BigFloat:(to-json 1//3)                         # => "#rat:1/3"
(eq? (from-json (to-json big"1.5")) big"1.5")   # => true

Definitions in air are patterns: a form with wildcards that, when it matches
a subject, supplies a replacement. A def installs one globally; a replacement
rule in head position acts as a function; and the same pattern language drives
replace, case, map, and the other traversal verbs. This chapter covers the
pattern language and everything built on it.

Any form is a pattern, but a form without wildcards matches only itself.

Wildcards: Symbols starting with ? stand for any value and evaluate to
themselves in patterns.

Conditions (\): The character \ stands for “such that” and introduces
a condition (e.g., (?h \ string? 10) or (?h \ (string? h) 10)).

Alternatives (|): A pipe joins two adjacent elements into (alt p q);
a run flattens, so p | q | r is (alt p q r). Branches are tried in order
and the first match wins, with that branch’s bindings (a failed branch leaks
nothing). alt is pattern syntax, not an anchor: a rule is indexed by the
raw symbols inside its branches.

Rest & Sequences: ?? matches any other elements; ??rest binds all
sequential and keyword sequences while ?&rest, and ?*kwargs bind
variable-length sequential or keyword sequences respectively.

Optional Keyword Patterns: Keys starting with a ? (e.g.,
?method=naught) are optional and bind to a default value (naught in this
case) if missing. However, the keyword matched in this example is :method,
not ?method.

hierarchy.lvl2: Global vs. Local Patterns & The Anchor Rule
Global vs. Local Patterns & The Anchor Rule

records.content:
Global Evaluation Rules: To guarantee blazing-fast indexation in the RETE
engine, every global pattern must include at least one raw (non-keyword and
non-wildcard) symbol anchor (e.g., (f ?x) is valid; (?f ?x) or (?x 1)
are invalid globally).

Local Structural Patterns: Purely structural, unanchored patterns are
fully permitted when explicitly invoked via local operations (e.g.,
(replace dataset ((?a ?b) ?c) (a b c))).

Functions and reduction rules can name parameters that are matched raw and
inserted into the replacement exactly as matched using the hold=(...) option
in def. Such a parameter is bound to the raw form for the duration of one
replacement — it is not held, and it is not evaluated at binding time; a
non-held parameter is reduced first. The replacement then reduces normally, so
the raw match is visible to the rules that immediately enclose it and is
evaluated in due course otherwise. An explicit (unhold x) evaluates a raw
match inside the body (~ is a quasiquote hole and is a different operation),
and a held occurrence 'x receives the held match.

Example — raw argument insertion:(def (f ?x ?y) hold=x (g x y))
(f (1 + 1) (2 + 2))          # => (g (1 + 1) 4), then (g 2 4)
(let (x=5 y=6) (f x y))      # => (g 5 6) (let substitutes before the rule runs)

A def with no body declares a rule that reproduces its matched form rather
than replacing it, so the form itself becomes a fixed point. The parameters are
still inserted according to the usual rule — a non-held parameter reduces, a
hold= parameter is inserted raw — but nothing else reduces:(def (f ?x))                 # arguments reduce, the form does not
(f (1 + 1))                  # => (f 2)
(def (g ?x) hold=x)          # the argument is inserted exactly as matched
(g (1 + 1))                  # => (g (1 + 1))

The replacement is the pattern with each matched part put back in place: an
unnamed ? contributes its reduced match, a rest marker splices the remaining
elements, and an optional key contributes the subject’s entry (or is omitted
when absent).

A def body inherits the whole do grammar. It may use level-1 :let
markers, take the let= and catch= options, and end with except, handle,
and finally clauses; several body forms are evaluated in sequence as a do
block. A body that needs none of those is stored exactly as written, so an
ordinary one-form definition is unchanged:(def (recip ?x)
  catch=:zero
  (if (== x 0) (throw :zero :undefined) (/ 1 x)))

(recip 4)                 # => 0.25
(recip 0)                 # => :undefined

(def (lookup d k)
  let=(missing=:absent)
  (notify :miss k)
  (handle (:miss ?key) missing))

The option tx=true runs the body in a transaction, making the definition
equivalent to a tx instead of a do: an error escaping the body aborts every
write it made, while an error caught by the body’s own except (or a throw
caught by its own catch=) commits. tx=false is the default, an ordinary
block. let=, catch=, and tx=true need a non-empty body.

val accepts the same options and body grammar; its value is evaluated once at
definition time.

A def may take memoize=m to cache results by the evaluated arguments:

memoize=true or memoize=:weak (the default mode) holds each result
weakly: an entry survives only while another value still references the
result, so the cache never pins memory.

memoize=(:lru max) holds up to max results strongly, evicting the least
recently used entry.

memoize=false or memoize=naught disables memoization, which is the
default when the option is absent.

The key is the rule’s evaluated parameter bindings, compared by eq?
equivalence: (f (+ 1 1)) and (f 2) share an entry, (f 1) and (f 1.0) are
distinct, and equal maps written in a different order are the same key. A held
parameter contributes its raw match, exactly as the body sees it. The mode is stored with the definition in its namespace and is
reproduced by definitions; the cache itself is process-local and never saved.
A redefinition starts a fresh cache. An implicit def (no body) cannot be
memoized, and memoization assumes the body is deterministic — a result that
depends on a mutable, the current user, or another dynamic context will be
reused. A memoized result is computed eagerly, so recursive calls inside a
memoized rule do not occupy tail position.(def (fib ?n) memoize=true
  (if (< n 2) n (+ (fib (- n 1)) (fib (- n 2)))))
(fib 80)                  # => 23416728348467685

Example — Fibonacci Sequence (Reduction Rule):(def (f ?n)
  (if (= n 0) 1
      (= n 1) 1  # automatic else-if
      (+ (f (- n 1)) (f (- n 2)))))

Example — Held argument:(def (diff (?a + ?b) ?a)
  (1 + (diff (unhold b) (unhold a))))
(def (duff (?b + ?a) ?a)
  ((diff b a) + 1))

hierarchy.lvl2: Lambdas: A Replacement Rule in Head Position
Lambdas: A Replacement Rule in Head Position

records.content:
There is no separate lambda form: a replacement rule in head position is a
function. Its pattern is matched against the arguments as written — no
arguments is naught, one argument is that argument, and several are the
argument list — and its replacement is the body:((?x -> (x ^ 2)) 3)              # => 9
(((?a ?b) -> (a + b)) 3 4)       # => 7
(let (f=(?x -> (x + 1))) (f 2))  # => 3

A multi-parameter pattern needs its own parentheses — the rule form has exactly
three elements, so (?a ?b -> body) is not a rule. A call whose pattern does
not match is left unreduced, and such a form passed to map, filter,
reduce, sort-by, and the other higher-order verbs is applied element by
element.

The body is substituted, not lexically closed: free names in the replacement
resolve when the rule is applied, in the caller’s scope — (let (x=2) ((?y -> (x + y)) 3)) → 5. A name bound by the pattern shadows an outer binding of the
same name. Rule data is opaque to scope resolution and to let: neither rewrites
the pattern, and the replacement is rewritten only where the pattern does not
bind the name.

Inside the body, _ is bound to a hold of every argument as it entered:((?x -> _) 5)                    # => '5
(((?a ?b) -> _) 5 6)             # => (' 5 6)
((?x -> _) (a b))                # => (' (a b))

In a replace rule (and in a case clause) _ is instead the entire matched
subject, unheld: (replace (abc 1) ((? \ symbol? 1) -> (row=_))) →
(row=(abc 1)). A replacement rule also accepts unhold=true, which inserts its
replacement unheld so the result is evaluated.

Partial application is the part form: (part f a b) captures f, a, and
b (holding them so they are not reduced) and applying the result appends the
new arguments — ((part add 10) 5) is (add 10 5). partial is not a separate
verb; use part. The companions comp (compose), juxt (apply all and
collect), and complement (negate a predicate) follow the same rule.

(case subject clause… default?) evaluates the subject once and tests each
clause in order. A clause is a replacement rule, using the ordinary pattern
language — wildcards, \ conditions, nested patterns, and _ for the whole
subject — so a clause can discriminate structurally, not just by equality:(case (abc 1) ((? \ symbol? 1) -> (row=_)) :other)   # => (row=(abc 1))
(case (a b) ((?n \ integer?) -> (n * 2)) ((?a ?b) -> (a + b)))  # => (a + b)

The first matching clause’s replacement is evaluated and returned so a matching
clause in tail position is a tail call. A trailing element that is not a
replacement rule is the default, returned as-is when nothing matches; without one
the result is naught. A non-rule element anywhere but last is an error.
select is an alias.

replace, rreplace, map, cases, and drop-cases accept depth=n, which
selects the level of the form they operate on. depth=0 is the subject itself;
depth=n is every node n element steps down, where both sequence elements and
map values are children, with the structure above the selected level rebuilt.
A scalar is its own sole element (the same “a scalar is a singleton” convention
the collection verbs use), so descending past a scalar stays on it; an extern is
opaque. replace and rreplace default to depth=0; map, cases, and
drop-cases default to depth=1.(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x))          # => ((a 1) (a 2))  (depth 0)
(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x) depth=1)  # => (1 2)
(map (?x -> (wrap x)) (a=(1 2) b=3) depth=2)
# => (a=((wrap 1) (wrap 2)) b=(wrap 3))

replace-all and rreplace-all keep their whole-tree walk when depth is
absent; given depth=n, they operate only on level n (so depth=0 is then
exactly replace).

(cases coll clause… depth=n) collects the elements at that level that match a
clause, in encounter order. A clause is a bare pattern (the element itself is
kept) or a replacement rule (pattern -> replacement) (the element is
replaced); a rule-level guard (p \ g) on a bare pattern tests the whole
element, so (?x \ even?) selects even elements. Non-matching elements are
omitted. (drop-cases coll clause… depth=n) returns the collection with the
matching elements removed and the rest of the structure rebuilt:(cases (1 2 3 4) (?x \ even?))                 # => (2 4)
(cases (1 2 3 4) ((?x \ even?) -> (10 * x)))   # => (20 40)
(drop-cases (1 2 3 4) (?x \ even?))            # => (1 3)
(drop-cases (a=1 b=2 c=3) (?x \ even?))        # => (a=1 c=3)

Unlike case, cases and drop-cases have no default clause: a bare pattern
is indistinguishable from one.

(matches-any? subject clause…) asks the same question over the whole tree:
it is true when the subject itself or any subpart matches a clause. Clauses are
as in cases — a bare pattern, a rule-level guard, or a replacement rule (only
its pattern and guard matter):(matches-any? (a (b 1)) b)             # => true
(matches-any? (1 3) (?x \ even?))      # => false

(nest f n x) applies f to x exactly n times; (nest-list f n x) returns
every value along the way, from x to the final one (n + 1 elements).
(nest-while f pred x) applies f while pred holds of the current value,
testing before each application, so a value that already fails is returned
unchanged; list=true returns the values instead of the last one.(nest (?x -> (2 * x)) 5 1)                      # => 32
(nest-list (?x -> (2 * x)) 3 1)                 # => (1 2 4 8)
(nest-while (?x -> (div x 2)) even? 8)           # => 1
(nest-while (?x -> (div x 2)) even? 8 list=true) # => (8 4 2 1)

The count n must be a non-negative integer. f and pred take a symbol
naming a rule or a lambda, as the other higher-order verbs do; a predicate that
never fails is stopped by the reduction budget.

A literal string at the head of a def body is that rule’s docstring; it is
removed from the executable body. A multiline docstring is deindented: leading
and trailing blank lines are dropped and the continuation lines lose their
common indentation.(def (log ?x \ number?)
  "Returns the natural log of x."
  ...)

(def (log ?base \ number? ?x \ number?)
  "Returns the log-base-b of x."
  ...)

(doc symbol) returns a terminal-ready string listing every documented pattern
that uses the symbol, and (doc (form…)) — which holds its argument rather
than evaluating it — lists the documented patterns that match that form:(doc log)          # both patterns above, each with its docstring
(doc (log 1.0))    # only the one-argument pattern

(definitions arg) takes the same argument and returns the matching def forms
as quoted data instead, moving each docstring from the head of the body into a
doc= map entry:(definitions log)
# => ((' def (log ?x \ number?) ... doc="Returns the natural log of x.")
#     (' def (log ?base \ number? ?x \ number?) ... doc="Returns the log-base-b of x."))

Undocumented rules are included too, just without a doc= entry. Because the
returned forms are live quoted data, rule bodies should use (unhold x) for
runtime unholding (it is an ordinary call and survives reconstruction verbatim)
and lift to build a computed quoted form. A ~ is a quasiquote hole: a body
that is itself quoted code containing ~ has that hole expanded when the
reconstruction’s quote is built, so use lift there too if the body must
survive as data.

Air’s namespaces are multi-user. A user id is a keyword: :air, :alice,
:game:bob. Name segments are [A-Za-z0-9_-]+ with no leading digit, no
leading - followed by a digit, and not the single _. A constituent id is
exactly admin:name (one level; a constituent cannot itself have
constituents). :air is the implicit superuser:
it passes every permission check, creates core users, and is the only user that
may change admin status.

(current-user) is the task’s identity (default :air), and (owner) is the
owner of the def currently executing, else the current user. (as-user id body…) evaluates body as id for its dynamic extent; authentication is out
of scope, so this is the whole mechanism for acting as another user. (users)
lists the users visible to the task — the system users, or the attached
database’s users while @ is set.(create-user :bob)                       ; :air only
(set-admin :game true)                   ; :air only
(as-user :game (create-constituent :kid)) ; => :game:kid
(as-user :game:kid (current-user))        ; => :game:kid

Each user has a home namespace, $: a top-level def run as that user is
written there. System users’ records live in .sys.user.<name>; database
users’ live in @.user.<name>. The home is a capability: $ is reachable even
when the enclosing record is not, and air’s .main stays private.

Every namespace and every namespace entry is a volatile whose metadata carries
an owner and an ACL:(owner=:alice
 acl=(read=(_=true bob=true)
      write=(alice=true)
      exec=(_=true)
      readfact=(_=true)
      writefact=(alice=true)
      readrule=(_=true)
      writerule=(alice=true)
      assume=(game:bob=true)
      hide=(mallory=true)
      watch=(alice=true)
      filter=(alice=true)
      finalize=(alice=true)))

Each permission maps user ids to booleans; :_ means every user. By default the
owner has read, write, exec, the four fact/rule permissions, watch,
filter, and finalize, and nobody else has anything. air bypasses every
check, and a core admin has ownership privileges over its constituents’ data.
hide is a veto: a listed user has no access of any kind. watch gates
installing a watch (which also needs read); filter and finalize gate
replacing a mutable’s filter or finalizer. anchor=true is a per-entry flag
rather than a permission — it forces imports of that entry to be proxies (see


using, use, and import).
filesystem is different from the rest: no policy grants it, it is checked on
the system namespace .air.sys rather than on an entry, and it admits the
holder to the host-path tools (see 

the filesystem).

The four fact/rule permissions govern a namespace’s implicit logic set (see


logic sets): readfact/readrule for
facts, rules, why, and query, and writefact/writerule for
assert, retract, revise, and revise-fact. A standalone logic-set handle
keeps the older mapping, where those operations need the set’s read or
write.

(permissions target) returns the metadata, (chmod! target read=(…) write=(…) exec=(…) readfact=(…) writefact=(…) readrule=(…) writerule=(…) assume=(…) hide=(…) watch=(…) filter=(…) finalize=(…) filesystem=(…) anchor=…) replaces
the listed permission maps, and (chown! target user) gives the target a new
owner. A
target is a namespace, a definition (by name or by (get …)), or a mut.
chmod! and chown! need write on the target.

operation

requires

get/printing/doc of an entry’s body

read on the entry

calling a def

exec on its entry (and read on the namespace to reach its map)

resolving or binding a val

read on its entry

def/val/clear/unuse in a namespace

write on the namespace

(namespace ns …)

read on ns; writes additionally need write

chmod!/chown!

write on the target

assert/retract/revise/revise-fact on a namespace

writefact, or writerule for a rule form

facts/rules/why/query on a namespace

readfact, readrule, or both as used (why needs both)

reading/writing a mut

read/write on the mutable

watch/unwatch/watches

watch (and read for watch) on the mutable

set-filter!/set-finalize!

filter/finalize on the mutable

read-file/write-file/load-air/read-data/write-data

filesystem on .air.sys

(open-airdb …)

write on the containing namespace

A denial is a catchable error object, (error :permission-denied :read|:write|:exec|:readfact|:writefact|:readrule|:writerule|:assume target),
whose content an except clause matches as
(:permission-denied perm target), where target is a namespace path or a keyword name. Operations that
filter — using, doc, definitions, namespace printing — treat an
unreadable entry as absent rather than raising, and printing shows the body as
#<entry …>.

(assume body…) is legal only inside a def whose entry grants assume to the
current user. It evaluates body with current-user set to that definition’s
owner, so an owner can expose a controlled operation on private data without
granting read or write on the data itself:(namespace .vault
  (val hidden 41)
  (def (peek) (assume hidden)))
(chmod! .vault read=(_=true) exec=(_=true))          ; the namespace is reachable
(chmod! (get . :vault :peek) exec=(_=true) assume=(bob=true))
(as-user :bob (.vault.peek))      # => 41; bob cannot read hidden directly

(env) returns the task’s environment mapping, and (with-env mapping body…)
extends it for the dynamic extent of body. Both .env and val bindings
travel into a task; (task clean=true …) starts with empty bindings and
an empty .env but keeps identity and namespace context.

Ordinary users have no filesystem. The tools that touch a host path directly —
read-file, write-file, load-air, read-data, and write-data — are
gated by the filesystem permission on .air.sys. No namespace policy
grants that permission, so a fresh instance admits only air, which owns the
namespace and bypasses every check; any other identity, including an admin or a
constituent, is refused until it is granted:(create-user :bob)
(as-user :bob (read-file "/etc/hosts"))   # raises (:permission-denied :filesystem :read-file)
(as-user :bob (read-data "conf.toml"))    # raises (:permission-denied :filesystem :read-data)

(chmod! .air.sys filesystem=(bob=true))   # air grants bob the filesystem
(as-user :bob (read-file "/etc/hosts"))   # now reads
(chmod! .air.sys filesystem=(bob=false))  # and revokes it

Only air may change the grant: chmod! needs write on .air.sys, which the
namespace policy gives to nobody else. (permissions .air.sys) shows the
filesystem mapping once it exists. The grant admits a user to every host-path
helper, not to one function.

The refusal is a catchable error object, so an except clause matches
(:permission-denied :filesystem name) where name is the function.

Configuration is therefore read at startup, by air, rather than on demand by
a user; a library’s init.air also runs as air, so it needs no grant. Data
that users share travels through namespaces, bytes (over 

SSH/SFTP),
and databases, never through a host path. In-memory conversion — decode and
encode — operates on a string or a bytes value, touches no file, and needs
no permission at all.

Air values are printed as air source: what you write is what you read back. Two
printers serve different needs — the flat printer, which is what forms mean,
and the pretty printer, which breaks a form across lines to fit a width.
A layout declaration tells the pretty printer how a particular shape of form
should break.

air_string(x) is the flat spelling: one line, every map entry after the
sequence elements, in the canonical order. air_pretty_string(x; width=80) is
the same text broken across lines to fit width, and it is identical to the
flat spelling when the form already fits. Both are Julia functions; in air, the
form->string verb is the same pair:(form->string x)                               # flat
(form->string x pretty=true width=22)          # broken to fit 22 columns

For x the form (foo (alpha 1) (beta 2)), the second is(foo (alpha 1)
 (beta 2))

The REPL prints results with the pretty printer at the terminal’s width. The
air command reads COLUMNS and passes it through; the default is 80. In
Julia, both air_string(env, x) and air_pretty_string(env, x; width=…) respect
the current user’s permissions (an unreadable entry prints as a handle).

The greedy rule is simple: print elements on the current line while they fit,
and start a new line when the next one would exceed the width. The head
elements are pinned to the opening line; the rest start at the indent column.
A form that fits entirely stays on one line, so the printer never spends more
vertical space than it needs.

A layout is an ordinary air form:(layout (myverb ?first ?&rest) head=2 indent=2 map=block)

PATTERN selects the forms to lay out. It is matched structurally — the
same wildcards and rest markers as a 

def pattern — against the
form’s shape, before any evaluation. It may contain literals, wildcards, and
one rest marker, which must be the last pattern element. It may not use \
conditions (there is no scope available while printing), and it may not carry
map entries.

head=N pins the first N sequence elements to the opening line (default 1).
(def (f ?x) …) uses head=2, so the name and its arguments stay together.

indent=M puts continuation lines M columns past the opening ( (default
1). indent=align instead aligns them with the column where the last pinned
element starts.

map=block puts every key=value entry on its own line; map=inline (the
default) packs them like the other elements.(layout (myverb ?first ?&rest) head=2 indent=2 map=block)

(layout (myverb ?first ?&rest) head=2 indent=2)   # declare (or replace)
(layouts)                                         # the declarations, newest last
(clear-layout :myverb)                            # drop the ones for one head
(clear-layout :all)                               # drop every user declaration

Registering a pattern identical to an existing declaration replaces it, so
evaluating a declaration twice is harmless. The built-in defaults cannot be
removed — clear-layout only drops your own declarations, after which the
default (or the generic layout) applies again.

A layout is a process-global registration, not a definition: (sandbox …)
does not undo one, and it is not part of a transaction. That is deliberate —
layouts describe how code is displayed, not what the code does — so keep them
in startup code or a library rather than in a transaction whose outcome matters.

Layouts are also purely presentational: the flat air_string is unaffected, and
pretty output re-reads as exactly the same form as the flat output — reading
(form->string x pretty=true) and (form->string x) with string->form gives
two eq? values.

This document specifies the RETE-based deductive rule engine (logic-set):
the rule form, its instructions, the trigger model, and aggregation/grouping
with :accum.

Air blends symbolic code-as-data structures with deductive rule evaluation. A
rule is a single structured form whose conditions are an implicit
conjunction and whose instructions say what to derive and what side effects
to run. Consequences are written as explicit :> slots, so the engine can
track each derived fact across firings; aggregation is a condition-region
:accum declaration rather than boilerplate.(rule (student class=?c grade=?g)
      :accum (g=:mean)
      :> (average class=?c value=?g))

Rules are asserted into a logic-set like any other value:(assert s (rule (parent ?x ?y) :> (ancestor ?x ?y)))

(rule cond1 cond2 … :if g :let (k=v …) :> f :+ f :- f := f …)

Conditions are the leading elements up to the first instruction keyword.
They are an implicit conjunction: (rule (parent ?x ?z) (ancestor ?z ?y) …).
(not p) requires that no matching fact exists. :accum may appear anywhere
in the condition region and applies to the whole conjunction.

Instructions are keyword/argument pairs interpreted in order:

:if cond — if the reduced condition is not truthy, none of the
instructions that follow are executed. A :> skipped this way counts as
having produced naught.

:let (k1=v1 k2=v2 …) — evaluate and bind names as in let. Bindings
within one map are parallel; separate :let instructions are sequential,
so later ones see earlier values.

:> form — a consequence. Reduced with the bindings, it must yield a fact
or naught. Each :> has a fixed slot index (its position among the :>
instructions) that identifies the derived fact across firings.

:+ form, :- form, := form — side effects run on an assertion,
retraction, or revision trigger, respectively. They may call assert,
retract, revise, or revise-fact only with an explicit reason=; :>
needs none, because its output is automatically a derived fact.

At least one condition and one instruction are required. Rules enter a
logic-set held and are never reduced as code.

The condition decides the trigger; the consequences do not:

event

when

instructions that run

assertion

a new combination of conditions matches

:if, :let, :>, :+

revision

a matching combination persists but a matched fact was revised (or an accumulator group changed)

:if, :let, :>, :=

retraction

a matching combination stops matching

:if, :let, :- (old bindings)

In :=, the special symbol _ is bound to a map-form of the revised condition
wildcards to their new values.

Facts carry stable identity tokens. Each (invocation, :> slot) remembers its
last output, and the old/new pair classifies the event:

naught → fact: assert the fact with derived provenance.

fact → naught: retract it when no other reason holds it.

two different facts: revise — if the old fact has no other reason, its
identity moves to the new value; otherwise the old fact stays and the new one
is asserted.

equal facts: no event.

Only :> outputs drive downstream events. A revised fact keeps its identity,
so a rule matching it fires its revision trigger (:=) rather than being
retracted and re-asserted. Consequences therefore decide their own fact events;
the condition event only selects which side effects run.

A fact exists while it has at least one reason record:

a base record, labelled with the reason= given to assert (default
naught) or a keyword; and

a derived record, (because RULE PREMISE-FACT…), one per deriving
(invocation, :> slot).

Labels may be shared across facts and an assertion is its own record. Retracting
or revising one record leaves the fact present if another reason still holds
it. (why s fact) returns every reason. revise and revise-fact target base
facts only.

:accum lists the accumulated variables. Every other bound variable is a
group key.

(rule (student class=?c grade=?g)
      :accum (g)
      :> (all class=?c grades=?g))

?c is a scalar group key; ?g binds to a vector of the group’s grades.

(rule (student class=?c grade=?g) :accum (g=:mean) :> (average class=?c value=?g))

Unannotated listed variables stay vectors. The aggregators are :min, :max,
:sum, :mean, :median, :first, and :last.

:take (min v), :take (max v), :take :first, and :take :last bind all
listed variables to the selected row’s scalars instead of vectors:(rule (student class=?c grade=?g) :accum (c g :take (max g))
      :> (best class=?c grade=?g))

:take :last is optimized to track the latest match directly rather than
collecting every value.

Repeated :accum specs nest. Outer levels partition; only the final level
aggregates or takes, yielding parallel sequences. In(rule (student class=?c dept=?d grade=?g)
      :accum (d) :accum (g=:mean)
      :> (roll class=?c depts=?d means=?g))

?c is the scalar group key, ?d binds to the sequence of departments for that
class, and ?g binds to a sequence of mean grades aligned with ?d. An
annotation or :take on a non-final level is an error.

:first and :last follow assertion order. A revision preserves a fact’s
position in its group.

:if gates the instructions, so an aggregated group can be filtered before its
consequence fires:(rule (student class=?c grade=?g)
      :accum (g=:mean)
      :if ((mean ?g) > 85)
      :> (honor-roll class=?c avg=(mean ?g)))

Flipping a group in and out of the guard asserts and retracts the consequence,
respectively.

(revise s condition changes) rewrites every base fact matching condition;
changes is a (k=v …) map from the condition’s wildcards to new values.
(revise-fact s old new) names the facts directly. Both take an optional
reason= naming which record moves. A condition matching nothing is a no-op;
matching only derived facts is an error.(revise s (stats player=?p health-points=?h) (h=90) reason=:damage)

A revision moves the fact’s reason record and identity, so the fact is not
retracted and re-asserted: downstream rules receive a revision trigger and run
their := side effects.

(logic s edit…) applies a group of edits as one event. Reads inside the block
see the set as it stood on entry, per-fact revision chains collapse within the
call (a later revise follows the moved record), and an error rolls the whole
block back. Two successive logic calls do not collapse.

Air features two complementary rule systems tailored for algebraic evaluation
and declarative logic programming, respectively.

The inner system handles bottom-up algebraic evaluation, function definition
(def), syntax normalization, and immediate fixed-point reduction. When a form
like (f 2) is submitted to the evaluation engine, reduction rules evaluate it
recursively until a fixed point is reached.

The outer system operates like a DROOLS rules engine backed by logic-set
objects.

Logic Sets: Every namespace is a logic set, and logic-set makes a
standalone one. Users add, change, and remove facts with (assert s fact),
(retract s fact), (revise s condition changes), and (revise-fact s old new); with no target they edit the current namespace. defrule asserts a
structured rule, query lists the satisfiers of a condition block, and
ingest copies the base facts and rules of another set. Operations take an
optional reason= — naught (the default) or a keyword. revise changes
only base facts: the condition binds wildcards and the (k=v …) map gives
their new values.

-> is replacement-only. (pattern -> replacement) is inert data for the
replace family (see below); it is not a rule in the outer system. A form
containing -> asserted into a logic-set is an ordinary fact.

Rules are structured forms. A RETE rule is
(rule conditions… instructions…): the leading forms are an implicit
conjunction (negation is (not pattern)), and the rest is a flat sequence of
keyword/argument instruction pairs interpreted by the engine:(assert s (rule (parent ?x ?z) (ancestor ?z ?y)
                :if (not (done ?x))
                :let (label=(concat x "/" y))
                :> (ancestor ?x ?y)
                :+ (log "new")
                :- (log "gone")
                := (log _)))

:if cond — if the condition is not truthy, the instructions after it are
skipped (a skipped :> is naught).

:let (k=v …) — bind names as in a let; later instructions see them.
Separate :let instructions are sequential, while bindings inside one map
are parallel.

:> form — a consequence: the form must reduce to a fact or naught. Each
:> has a fixed slot that identifies its output across firings.

:+ form, :- form, := form — side effects run on an assertion,
retraction, or revision trigger. They may call assert/retract/revise/
revise-fact only with an explicit reason=. During := the wildcard _
is bound to a map of the changed wildcards to their new values.

Triggers are decided by the condition, not by the consequence:
a new combination of matches is an assertion (runs :if, :let, :>,
:+); a combination that persists while a matched fact was revised (or an
accumulator group changed) is a revision (runs := instead); a
combination that stops matching is a retraction (runs :- with the old
bindings). Each :> slot’s old and new outputs classify its own event:
naught→fact asserts, fact→naught retracts, different facts revise, equal
facts do nothing. Facts carry stable identities across revisions, so a
downstream rule sees a revision rather than a retract/assert pair.

Reasons. Every fact exists because of one or more reason records. A base
fact records the label given to assert/revise (a keyword or naught); a
derived fact records (because RULE PREMISES…). Labels may be shared, and a
fact survives while any reason holds it; retracting or revising one reason
touches only that record. (why s fact) returns every reason.

Grouping and accumulation (:accum). :accum lists the accumulated
variables; every other bound variable is a group key:(assert s (rule (student class=?c grade=?g)
                :accum (g=:mean)
                :> (avg class=?c value=?g)))

Unannotated variables bind to vectors; =:min, =:max, =:sum, =:mean,
=:median, =:first, and =:last aggregate. :take (min v), :take (max v), :take :first, and :take :last select one row instead. Repeated
:accum specs nest: outer levels partition and the final level aggregates,
yielding parallel sequences. :first/:last follow insertion order, and a
revision keeps its position.

Atomic blocks. (logic s edits…) applies a group of edits as one event:
reads inside the block see the snapshot from entry, per-fact revision chains
collapse within the call (but not across calls), and an error rolls the whole
block back.

Advanced Features: complete provenance tracking (a Justification-Based
Truth Maintenance System) that records why a fact is true so an LLM can
narrate explanations on demand.

In-Place Mutation & STM: Instead of destructive retract/reassert cycles
for mutable entities (like revising the fact
(stats player=:Nurgle health-points=100) to
(stats player=:Nurgle health-points=90)), revise moves the fact’s reason
record and identity in place, emitting a targeted delta.

Actor-Backed I/O: Side effects involving file descriptors or network
outputs are routed to background actors, ensuring safe rollback if STM
transactions abort.

An air process can serve SSH. A user logs in with a key listed in their own
configuration and lands as themselves, in their home namespace, at a REPL; the
same account serves SFTP, so scp and sftp move files in and out. A
transferred file is an immutable 

bytes
value and a directory is a namespace — there are no files in air, only paths.

The server is a process resource named by a key, like a task, not a value you
pass around:(ssh-server :myserver port=2222)
(ssh-servers)                     ; => (myserver=(owner=:air …))
(ssh-host-key :myserver)          ; the public key line, for known_hosts
(ssh-close! :myserver)            ; stop listening; keep the host key

Only air or an admin may start a server ((ssh-server) with no name generates
one, e.g. :ssh-3f9a1c2b), and a server admits exactly the users its owner may
assume: air admits everyone, and an admin admits itself and its constituents.
The admitted set is recomputed at each login, so a user created after the server
started can log in. (ssh-servers) lists the servers the caller may see — all
of them for air, its own for an admin.

Keys live in the user’s own home, under $.config.ssh, and the server options
come from the owner’s. The namespace shape:(create-user :alice)
(as-user :alice
  (namespace $.config.ssh
    (val authorized-keys
      ("ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIA… alice@laptop"))))

A server owner also sets the defaults its servers start with:(namespace $.config.ssh
  (val server (port=2222 bind="127.0.0.1" host-key-type="ed25519"
               max-connections=4 banner="air ssh" key-types=("ssh-ed25519"))))

The second accepted shape is a single ssh val in $.config:(namespace $.config
  (val ssh (authorized-keys=("ssh-ed25519 AAAA… alice@laptop"))))

The namespace wins where both are present, and the two need not hold the same
entries. authorized-keys is a list; each entry is an OpenSSH one-line string
with no options (an entry with options, or one naming an unknown type, is
rejected with an error naming the user) or a mapping
(type="ssh-ed25519" key="AAAA…" comment="…"). A user with no readable entry
simply cannot log in.

Options are merged defaults < the owner’s $.config.ssh.server < the explicit
call, and (ssh-server …)'s own options are the same set:

option

default

meaning

port

2222

the listening port; 0 picks a free one

bind

"127.0.0.1"

the address to listen on

host-key-type

"ed25519"

the generated host key’s type (ed25519 or rsa)

key-types

()

client key types allowed to authenticate at all; empty allows any

max-connections

4

concurrent sessions per server

banner

"air ssh"

the protocol banner

The host key is generated on first use and stored in the process database at
.sys.ssh.<key>, so no file exists on disk and (ssh-close! :myserver) followed
by a new (ssh-server :myserver …) is the same host. (ssh-host-key :myserver)
returns the public line (put it in known_hosts), and private=true the
private key; reading either needs air or the server’s owner.

A POSIX login name cannot contain :, so the client name maps . to : —
alice is :alice, air.bob is :air:bob, game.kid is :game:kid:ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 alice@localhostair> (current-user)
:alice
air> (def (twice ?x) (x * 2))
naught
air> (exit)

Public-key authentication is the only method; a password is never accepted and
never offered. Every refusal — an unknown user, a wrong key, a user outside the
server’s scope, a malformed config — looks the same to the client, so the server
does not enumerate its users, and the connection is dropped after six failed
attempts.

The session is the local REPL with a line editor: history (Up/Down), Ctrl-A,
Ctrl-E, Ctrl-K, Ctrl-U, Ctrl-W, arrow keys, Home/End, and Delete, with
the prompt and results redrawn over the terminal width the client reports.

An incomplete form continues on the next line under a ...>  prompt.

Ctrl-C evaluates (raise :ctrl-c): the line being edited is discarded and
the error is printed, and the session continues. Evaluation is not
preemptible, so a byte sent while a form runs is read when that form finishes.

Ctrl-D on an empty line, a channel EOF, and (exit) all end the session.
(exit value) delivers value to the session task and prints nothing.

def and val typed at the prompt are written to the session user’s home
namespace, because $ is the current namespace there — durable, and readable
afterwards as air at .sys.user.<name>.home.….

Output goes to the client: (print …)/(println …) in a session write to the
channel, including from a task the session spawns. There is no
non-interactive exec: ssh host command is refused (it opens a channel request
air does not serve).

A remote path is an air path. It is split on both . and /, empty segments
dropped; a leading . or / is absolute (a root path), and anything else is
relative to the session user’s $:

client path

air path

data.weights

$.data.weights

./data/weights

$.data.weights

.sys.user.alice.home.data.weights

the same namespace, spelled absolutely

/main.config

.main.config

Any .. in a path is rejected: a path never climbs, so an sftp batch that
does cd .. fails rather than escaping the home. REALPATH(".") answers the
session home in dotted absolute form (sys.user.alice.home), so a client that
canonicalizes a relative path still lands in the same place.

Directories are namespaces and files are bytes vals:

Listing a namespace shows its subnamespaces as directories and its vals as
files, each filtered by the caller’s read permission; a def is not a file
and is not listed. A val that does not hold bytes still lists (with size
0) but refuses to open.

OPEN for writing buffers the whole transfer and CLOSE installs it as one
new bytes val in a single transaction, creating missing parent namespaces.
Partial files never appear and a failed upload leaves nothing behind, but a
large upload is held in memory rather than streamed — see the limitations.

A destination holding anything but bytes is refused (OPEN/CLOSE/
REMOVE), so a transfer can never overwrite a definition or a config.

Because . separates path segments, dir/file.bin is the file namespace
holding the bin val inside dir: a directory’s contents are always one
level down. rmdir is not recursive, so an sftp batch removes
dir/file.bin, then dir/file, then dir.

SFTP is version 3 with no extensions. The modern scp (which uses SFTP) works;
the legacy protocol (scp -O, which asks the server to run a command) does not.

Buffered uploads. A written file is assembled in memory and committed at
CLOSE, because bytes is immutable. Transfers are correct and atomic but
not incremental.

No exec, no recursive delete. There is no command channel and RMDIR
requires an empty namespace.

Ctrl-C is not preemptive. It is delivered when the running form finishes.

Listening is opt-in per address. A server binds 127.0.0.1 unless told
otherwise; there is no host-key exchange with an external sshd and no
password or certificate authentication.

AirLang.jl currently implements the inner (reduction) system.

Implemented

The reader: atoms (symbols, keywords, wildcards, strings, raw strings
raw"…", regex literals r"…" with flags, numbers, booleans,
naught), parenthesized forms, the | pattern-alternative shorthand, # line comments
and nestable #| … |# block comments,
k=v mappings and hybrid forms, the . accessor (f.a.b reads as
(get f :a :b)), and the ... splat ((f a... b)) — parsed directly into
AirDB.Form values.

The reduction engine: anchor-indexed dispatch (a global pattern is anchored by
any raw symbol it contains, so (?a + ?b) is anchored by +), fixed-point
reduction, and runtime canonicalization of the empty form (() → naught).

Pattern matching: exact structural match, named wildcards (?x), rest
wildcards (?& sequence, ?* keywords, ?? any remaining elements),
alternatives (p | q, read as (alt p q)), and
conditions (pattern \ pred, which must evaluate to true); the anchor rule is
enforced at def.

Error handling: (error :tag …) is an inert error object (arguments are
never evaluated); (raise :tag data…) evaluates its arguments and throws
(error :tag data…), and raising a single error object throws it exactly.
A (do options… body… (except pattern body…)… (handle pattern body…)… (finally body…)) block matches each except pattern against the error’s
content (the object without its error head); a bare wildcard pattern
binds the whole object, and the reserved symbol reraise as an except
body’s final value resumes the original error through later clauses. do
also takes let= (a block scope) and level-1 :let markers, scoped
catch=/throw (a throw returns the block early; an unmatched one is
(error :uncaught-throw tag value)), and handle clauses for (signal …)
objects dispatched by (notify …)/(notify-or default …); a handler’s value
becomes notify’s value and execution continues. finally always runs and
its value is discarded. from= records automatic handling context (Python’s
__context__) and cause= an explicit transformation; showerror prints
the chain. Any internal AirLang or Julia error surfaces as
(error :internal <message>). An uncaught error aborts the enclosing STM
transaction; an error caught inside the transaction commits; a throw escaping
the transaction commits first and is rethrown. try has been removed (its
name is a tombstone that raises).

Diagnostics: the reader records each container’s character span, and a loader
(load-air, a library init.air, the CLI) installs it while evaluating, so
an uncaught error prints (at name:line:col) plus the source line; a loaded
def/val stores its definition site as src=(name=… line=… col=… text=…)
in the entry body, and the innermost executing definition wins. Positions are
best-effort (a bare REPL form has none) and never change the error object an
except matches. (trace body…) yields the body’s value or, on error, the
data form (:trace (error …) frames=(…)).

Held forms (code-as-data): a hold is a container headed by the ordinary symbol
' — (' a b c) — and holds each element as written. 'x is reader sugar
for (' x) when x is a scalar ('a, '5, ':a, '"abc"); '(…) is a
parse error. A hold of one scalar prints with the quote, any other prints
literally ((' a b c)). (hold e…) reduces to (' e…), (unhold x) drops
the head and evaluates the content, and ~e (sugar for (preval e)) is an
eagerly evaluated hole filled in inside any hold, at every depth and in each
nested hold separately ((let (x=2) (' a ~x b)) → (' a 2 b); a let
nonetheless substitutes its names textually, so (let (x=2) (' a x b)) is
also (' a 2 b)). get indexes the form as written — (get (' f a b) 2) is
f — and hold=true makes the root hold transparent and keeps the result
held, with a path walked without reducing intermediate values;
(with form k1 v1 … hold=true) replaces subforms, inserting values without
their own holds. Every operation with a primary form argument has a hold-
version (hold-get, hold-nth, hold-with, hold-wout, hold-push,
hold-push-in, hold-join, hold-join-in, hold-update, hold-held?, and
hold-thread) that always sees through the root hold and holds its result;
hold= selects the result’s heldness. held?, lower, and lift are the
remaining hold operations. The other accessors see the raw form
((first (' a b c)) → '). def and a replacement-rule lambda accept a
hold=(x y) / hold=x option, and patterns support optional ?k=default
keys.

Integer keys are uniform across get, nth, with, wout, update,
update-in, and held?: 0 is the whole form, 1…n index the sequence,
-1…-n count from the end, and a setter’s key n + 1 appends. Anything
further raises. update-in follows the deep path k1 … kn and yields a
missing key as naught to the function.

and non-numeric operands are left unevaluated (symbolic) — (1 + 2) → 3,
(x + y) → (x + y).

Special forms def, let, if/cond, do, throw, notify,
notify-or, get, match?, matches,
mut, set!, swap!/alter!, tx, sandbox, watch/unwatch/watches,

(replace, replace-all, rreplace, rreplace-all) with inert

and subdivide), compare/hash, string

Recursion & composition: loop/recur and while; general tail calls (a
call in tail position — the branch of an if, a let body, the last form of
a clause-free do (with or without :let/let=), a
when/unless body, the last operand of and/or, a rule body, or an
applied lambda body — is reduced iteratively, so a tail-recursive rule runs in

lambdas as replacement rules in head position, whose bodies resolve their free
names in the caller’s scope at application time; the >> pipeline, which
substitutes _ textually through raw
steps and reduces only the final form

((f 1) (f 2) (f 3))); and identity/constantly/comp/complement/

Namespaces: (namespace ns body…) with automatic subnamespaces, atomic
blocks, and later-definition priority; dotted . paths through the root .
and the core .air; (using spec… body…) (one namespace or a list, with

Users and permissions: task-local current-user/owner, (as-user …),
(create-user …), (create-constituent …), (set-admin …), (users),

Mutables: set! (including deep traversal), swap!/alter!, (get m); a

Data formats: decode/encode and read-data/write-data convert JSON,

core tags only) and refuses every other tag. TOML dates, times, and datetimes
become the marker forms (toml-date …), (toml-time …), and
(toml-datetime …). Emitters sort map keys; write-data defers to the

permission on .air.sys, which a fresh instance grants only to air; an
ungranted user is refused with (:permission-denied :filesystem name), and

Persistence: one database per namespace, so mut, logic sets, and named forms
agree on where a form lives; named-form/name-form!/named-forms with
aliases, create=, history=, per-database names, and the air/ prefix
reserved; logic-set ACLs (standalone sets use write to mutate and read to

An air-level test framework: (check expr) is a boolean truth test that records
inside a (test name body…), whose result is the inert data summary
(name=… pass=… fail=… failures=(…)); counters are task-local, so nested and
concurrent tests do not interfere.

A REPL (air_repl) and the air command line (bin/air). The REPL reads a
form across lines while the reader reports an unterminated form, string, or
block comment (a ...>  continuation prompt), prints results through
air_pretty_string(x; width=80) (greedy line breaking; pass pretty=false
for the flat form), and appends each complete input to the file named by
AIR_HISTORY for external line editors such as rlwrap. (exit [value]) ends
the enclosing task: the REPL returns the value, a loaded file stops, and a
task body delivers it to its promise.

SSH access: (ssh-server [name] opts…) serves a line-editing REPL and SFTP v3
to users who authenticate with a key from their own $.config.ssh (or the
ssh val of $.config). Only air or an admin may start one, and it admits
exactly the users its owner may assume; the host key lives in the process
database at .sys.ssh.<key>; (ssh-servers),
(ssh-host-key key [private=true]), and (ssh-close! key) manage the servers.
A directory is a namespace and a file is an immutable bytes val, so
scp/sftp transfer against air paths. An upload is buffered and committed
as one val at CLOSE, and there is no exec channel.

User interfaces: a UI is a tree of inert (ui …) forms (the head is reserved,
like error) covering the full widget catalog — boolean, text, numeric,
selection, action, display, and layout kinds. (ui-open [key] tree) creates
a named, owner-scoped instance and evaluates its parameters; on-change runs
a callback and assert maintains a fact in the namespace current at
instantiation, labeled per element so it never disturbs an identical fact
asserted elsewhere. (ui-values), (ui-value), (ui-set! :key :id v),
(ui-update! :key tree), (ui-dismiss! :key), (ui-close! :key),
(ui-instances), and (ui-run tree) drive it; (ui-render :key width=n) is
a deterministic text renderer, and (ui-show :key) is a full-screen
alternate-buffer terminal renderer over an SSH session (alternate screen,
reverse-video focus, validation on a status line, Esc to dismiss, Ctrl-C to
abort with (error :ctrl-c)).

Printing and layouts: air_string is the flat spelling and
air_pretty_string(x; width=80) the greedy line-broken one, with
(form->string x pretty=true width=n) in air; the REPL reads its width from
COLUMNS. (layout PATTERN head=N indent=M map=inline|block) declares a
structural layout for matching forms (user declarations ahead of the defaults
for def, let, val, if, cond, do, tx, namespace, using,
logic, rule, assert, and error), managed by (layouts),
(clear-layout :head|:all), and (reset-layouts). A layout is process-global
and not undone by a transaction or a sandbox.

Times: a time is the ordinary immutable form (time SECONDS) (UTC epoch
seconds), printed as ISO-8601; (now), (time x), (time-str t format= offset=),
time?, the arithmetic (time ± number is a time, time − time seconds,
ordering between two times), between?/before?/after?, and the lib/time
helpers.

The outer production-rule engine (core): every namespace is implicitly a logic
set (the hidden named form air/logic/<path>, created lazily), and
logic-set makes a standalone named one; assert, retract, revise, and
revise-fact edit facts and rules, saturating the set to a fixed point. Bare
operations target the current namespace (or the enclosing logic block), and
query, defrule, and ingest round out the namespace-facing forms. A rule is the structured
(rule conditions… instructions…) form: the conditions are an implicit
conjunction ((not pattern) negates, :accum groups), and the instructions
are :if, :let, :> (consequence slots), and the trigger side effects
:+ / :- / :=. The condition’s event — assertion, revision, or
retraction — decides which side effects run; each :> slot’s old and new
outputs classify its own fact event. Facts have stable identities across
revisions and one or more reasons: a base label (naught or a keyword) or a
derived (because RULE PREMISES…); (why s fact) returns them. :accum
lists the accumulated variables (unlisted bindings are group keys), with
=:min/=:max/=:sum/=:mean/=:median/=:first/=:last aggregators,
:take row selection, and nested specs that yield parallel sequences.
(logic s edits…) applies a block as one atomic event (snapshot reads,
per-call revision collapse, rollback on error); (update coll key f) is the
collection update. Facts and rules enter a logic-set held, so they are
immutable data: a later def cannot rewrite a stored rule, and
(facts s)/(rules s) return one held list — (' (parent :abe :bob)) for
one fact, (') for none — whose elements are the unheld facts, so a fact
is ordinary data inside the hold. The
incremental alpha/beta network is still deferred.

Extern objects: a host-level value (a promise, a regex) is a
first-class form leaf, built on AirDB’s FormExtern/ExternHandle and its
register_extern type registry. (extern :type payload) reconstructs one from
the payload its printed form carries, extern?/extern-type inspect one, and
an extern prints as (extern :type payload), so it round-trips through source
(a regex prints as its r"…"flags literal instead).
A regex is a value: equal source-and-flags pairs are interned to the same
extern, so they are eq? and same?; promises are identities. A bytes
value is an immutable octet string with content equality (so it hashes like a
value) that prints opaquely as #<bytes N>; it is the value a transferred
file holds.
Concurrency: (task form…), (deliver p v), and (await x); task
holds its arguments, runs them on another task, and immediately returns a
database-backed promise. await returns the final form’s value or rethrows
the task’s error. A task captures its enclosing lexical scope like a
closure, keeps the namespace context captured at creation, and inherits the
current task’s val bindings (see Namespaces). An unnamed extern has
no stored data, so persisting one writes it without an id and reading it back
yields a dead extern that prints #<extern :type (expired)>; touching one
raises the catchable air error (error :extern-expired :type). A spawned task runs
its own STM transaction, so two tasks mutating the same form conflict and retry.

Database reference forms: an actor, a promise, and a delay are database-backed
values (AirDB’s ActorForm, PromiseForm, DelayForm) with their own
serializations. (actor value history=…)/(send a fn)/(reset! a v),
(promise)/(deliver p v)/(ready? p), and (delay body…); get (and
value) force a delay and read an actor or a promise, so all three vanish on a
get path like a mutable. Delays capture the namespace context, active
using layers, val bindings, @, .env, and their free lexical names,
compute once, and persist the result in a database cell.

Streams: (stream maxsize=n) is a reusable FIFO persisted in the current
namespace’s database (AirDB’s StreamForm), (post s v timeout=n) appends the
envelope (obj sender=:user time=(time …)), and (fetch s meta=true timeout=n) removes the oldest object or envelope, with a timeout expiry as
naught. count, open?, stream?, and (close! s) inspect and close one;
the stream’s read/write ACL gates receiving and delivering. A stream is
opaque on a get path, compares by identity, prints as #<stream uuid>, and
serializes as the link "&uuid".

The outer engine’s incremental RETE alpha/beta network (a full re-derivation

Forms-as-functions querying ((f 1) on a collection returns its element).

Serializable tasks: a task is a process item, so only its promise is
stored (as a link until delivered, as its value afterwards). Storing the

Sockets and other extern types; pmap and higher-level parallel helpers built

Incremental SSH transfers and a non-interactive exec channel: an SFTP upload

Spec notes

. is reserved: it is the subform accessor, the namespace root, and the
splat, not a symbol character. On a form, . is pure syntactic sugar for
get: form.key reads as (get form :key) and f.a.b as (get f :a :b),
which get walks so it can be overridden. At the start of an atom, .
introduces a namespace path (., .air, .util.a read as (get . :util :a);
the leading dot is the root, .air is the core namespace). The accessor keys
are held: a bare suffix is the literal keyword, so f.a does not see a
variable a. ~ evaluates a single key — f.~k reads as (get f (preval k)),
and f.~a.b as (get f (preval a) :b). A numeric suffix indexes a sequence and
a written keyword (f.:a, f.:test) is kept as written.

An operator’s canonical form is infix, and operators are symbolic on
non-numeric operands. Because infix is binary, (1 + 2 + 3) is a five-element
form (write (+ 1 2 3) or (1 + (2 + 3))).

The symbol character set is extended to accept < and > (used by the
comparison operators but absent from the list above).

The anchor rule is enforced as “at least one raw symbol anywhere in the
pattern”, which admits infix patterns such as (?a + ?b).

Canonicalization is applied by the reducer, not by the reader or by equality.

Complex numbers use i, not Julia’s im. A no-space 4.4+2.0i (the i
attached to the number) is a single literal; the spaced (4.4 + 2.0i) is the
infix sum, which reduces to the same value. A complex prints as one atom,
4.4+2.0i, so it re-reads as one value.

The full AirDB numeric tower is supported — Int64, BigInt, Float64,
BigFloat, Rational{Int64}, Rational{BigInt}, ComplexF64, and
Complex{BigFloat} — with reader literals, an exact printer, widened
predicates, and AirDB’s equivalence. // is the exact rational constructor
and integer division is div. See 

Numbers.

A stream is a reusable first-in-first-out queue: one task posts objects to
it and another fetches them, in order, any number of times. Unlike a promise,
which is assigned once, a stream lives until it is closed and can deliver
arbitrarily many objects.

A stream is a database-backed value (AirDB.StreamForm) stored in the


namespace where it is created, so it follows the ordinary
persistence and transaction rules: every post and fetch is staged in the current
transaction and becomes visible at the commit.

(namespace .jobs (val q (stream)))

(stream) creates an unbounded stream. (stream maxsize=8) bounds the queue:
once it holds maxsize items, a post waits (see 

timeouts). A
stream prints as an opaque handle, #<stream 0b1e…>, and reading it —
(get q), (value q) — never consumes an item. (stream? x) tests the type.

form

meaning

(post s obj timeout=n)

append obj; needs write; returns the envelope

(fetch s)

remove and return the oldest object; needs read

(fetch s meta=true)

return the whole envelope instead of the object

(fetch s timeout=n)

return naught if nothing arrives within n seconds

the queued items (read)
