whether the stream still accepts deliveries (read)

(close! s)

stop the stream (write)

Each delivery is stored as an envelope: the object, the posting user, and
the instant.(namespace .jobs (val q (stream)))
(post .jobs.q :build)          # => (:build sender=:air time=(time "2026-10-29T06:43:02.663Z"))
(fetch .jobs.q)                # => :build

post stamps the sender and the time itself, so sender= and time= are not
options. (fetch s meta=true) returns the envelope, which is how a consumer
learns who posted an object and when:(get (fetch .jobs.q meta=true) :sender)   # => :air
(get (fetch .jobs.q meta=true) :time)     # => (time "2026-10-29T06:43:02.663Z")

An item that is not an envelope — a stream written through the AirDB API
directly — reads back unchanged in both modes.

timeout= is in seconds and bounds the wait in both directions:(fetch .jobs.q timeout=0.5)    # => naught when nothing arrives

A naught result means the wait expired; it does not mean the stream is
closed. On a bounded stream, a post that would block waits at most
timeout= seconds and then returns naught. Without a timeout, both block
until the operation can proceed.

Because naught is a legitimate object to deliver, (fetch s) reports both an
expiry and a delivered naught as naught. Use meta=true to tell them apart:
a delivery is an envelope, an expiry is naught.

(close! s) stops the stream. Items already queued can still be fetched; once
the queue is empty, fetch raises (error :stream-closed), and post raises it
immediately. close! needs write, because it changes what the stream accepts.

The stream object carries its own ACL, and the two directions map onto the two
basic permissions:

read — receive (fetch, count, open?);

write — deliver (post, close!).

The namespace entry that names the stream keeps its own permissions: a user must
be able to read the entry to reach the stream at all. Granting read on the
stream to another user therefore looks like this:(namespace .jobs (val q (stream)))
(chmod! .jobs read=(_=true) exec=(_=true))
(namespace .jobs (chmod! q read=(_=true) exec=(_=true)))   # the entry
(chmod! .jobs.q read=(bob=true))                            # the stream: receive only

Bob can now (fetch .jobs.q) but a post raises (error :permission-denied write :stream). Granting write=(bob=true) on the stream lets him deliver, and
the envelope then names him as the sender.

A post or fetch made inside a transaction is part of it: an aborted transaction
drops its posts, and a committed one keeps them, in commit order. The stream is
persisted in the namespace’s database, so a post made in one environment is
visible to a fresh environment over the same database.

A blocking stream operation inside an open transaction cannot see the
transaction’s own staged writes; give it a timeout= so it expires instead of
waiting for a commit that cannot happen. (Air reports a detected self-deadlock
as (error :stream-deadlock).)

Use (sync) outside the transaction to wait for a committed post to reach the
database before another process reads it.

A stream is an ordinary database value. (to-json s) always writes a link,
"&<uuid>", never the queue; (from-json …) resolves the link back to the same
stream. Two references to one stream are eq?; two streams created separately
are not, and (hash s) follows stream identity.

A consumer can run on its own task while the producer posts from the main one.
A task inherits the namespace context, so it can name the stream directly:(namespace .pipeline
  (val q (stream))
  (val c (task (list (fetch q) (fetch q) (fetch q)))))

(post .pipeline.q :a)
(post .pipeline.q :b)
(post .pipeline.q :c)

(await .pipeline.c)             # => (list :a :b :c)

Because a stream keeps its objects, the consumer may also start after the
producer, or drain in a loop:(for (i (1 2 3)) (post .pipeline.q (* i i)))
(loop (n 3 acc ())
  (if (== n 0) acc (recur (- n 1) (push acc (fetch .pipeline.q)))))

Air is a Lisp-like functional language whose heaviest inspirations are Clojure
and Mathematica. Its core evaluation operations are fundamentally those of a
symbolic algebra engine, but it typically reads like a Lisp cousin.

Air uses many of the aesthetic conventions of a Lisp-like language. The syntax
consists of symbols, strings, numbers, and forms which are nested using
parentheses. Forms are containers whose elements are whitespace-separated and
bracketed by parentheses, such as (1 2 3).

A vertical pipe joins two adjacent sequence elements into a pattern
alternative: (a |b) is the pattern (alt a b), and a run flattens, so
(a | b | c) is (alt a b c). The pipe binds only its immediate neighbours,
so (f a | b c) is (f (alt a b) c); a map entry is not a sequence element
and may stand on neither side of a pipe. Matching tries the branches in order
and the first match wins, with that branch’s bindings. There is no reader
shorthand for nesting a form inside the final element; write the parentheses.

Comments begin with the # character and extend to the end of the line.

Strings in Air are bracketed by double quotes (") or triple double quotes
(""") and use the same formatting rules as Julia’s strings. A raw string —
raw"…" or raw"""…""" — follows Julia’s raw-string rules: a backslash is
literal (only \" escapes a quote), so raw"\d+" is the three characters
\d+ without doubling every backslash.

A regex literal — r"…" or r"""…""" — is a raw string whose text is
compiled into a regular expression as it is read; the letters i, m, s,
x, and a immediately after the closing quote are flags. The literal builds
the same value as (regex "…" ["flags"]), so r"\d+"i and (regex "\\d+" "i") are equal, and the printer spells a regex back as the literal.

Numbers are formatted as in Julia: integers too large for Int64 are read as
BigInt, 1//3 is a rational literal, big"1.5" a BigFloat, 2i and
4.4+2.0i complex values, and Inf/-Inf/NaN are the non-finite floats.
See 

Numbers.

Symbols may be specified in two ways:

Standard Symbols: A sequence of alphanumeric characters plus the
characters +, -, *, /, _, !, ?, :, $, @, ^, &, =,
. that does not start with a number forms a symbol; for example, x,
abc123, and + are all valid symbols.

Special Symbols:

Any symbol whose name starts with a ? is considered a wildcard for
pattern matching.

Any symbol that starts with a : is considered a keyword, meaning it
cannot be redefined and always evaluates to itself (patterns also share
this property).

r"a+" (or, equivalently, (regex "a+"), with optional flags as in
(regex "a+" "i")) compiles a pattern; the result is an ordinary value that
prints as the literal r"a+"i and round-trips through source. Every string verb
that takes a pattern accepts
either a string, matched literally, or a regex value, matched as a regular
expression: string-split, string-replace, string-index-of,
string-contains?, and string-match?; regex? tests for a regex value.

string-find returns the first match as (match=… index=… groups=…), or
naught; string-find-all returns a sequence of those forms.

index is a 1-based character index (not a byte offset), and groups is a
sequence of the capture strings (naught when the pattern has none).

A regex replacement expands $0 (the whole match), $1…$n, and $name
(a named group); $$ is a literal dollar. A literal pattern’s replacement is
used exactly as written.

string-match? is the pattern-oriented spelling of string-contains?: it
is true when the pattern matches anywhere in the subject.

All atom types evaluate to themselves with the exception of symbols, which can
be bound to other values. Following a Wolfram-like logic regarding variables
and symbols, symbols that are not bound to a value are treated as other
atoms--—i.e., they evaluate to themselves.

All Air code is simultaneously a piece of code and a piece of data (code is
data). A function call like (f x) is just a form with two symbols (f and
x), but if a pattern has been defined that fires on a match to (f ?x), then
when the (f x) form is submitted to the Air interpreter, it is replaced with
whatever the pattern defines.

let takes a binding form as its second element, followed by a body:(let (x=1 y=2) (+ x y))       # => 3

The bindings in one mapping are parallel: every value is evaluated in the
enclosing scope, before any of the names is substituted. let then substitutes
each name by its value in the body textually, before the body is evaluated, so
it does not introduce a scope of its own — it rewrites the body. Substitution
reaches every occurrence, including occurrences inside a quoted form:(let (x=2) (' a x b))                    # => (' a 2 b)
(let (y=10) (let (x=y) (?y -> x)))        # => (?y -> 10)

The binding form may also be a sequence of mappings, each of which feeds the
next: names bound by earlier groups are substituted into later groups’ value
expressions before those are evaluated. Within a group the bindings stay
parallel, and a rebound name refers to its previous value inside its own new
value:(let ((a=1 b=2) (c=(a + b))) c)          # => 3
(let ((x=1) (x=(x + 2))) x)              # => 3

A hold=(x y) option on the let form names bindings whose values are inserted
exactly as written instead of evaluated (in every group; earlier groups still
substitute into them):(def (hold-y y=?y ??rest) hold=y)
(let (x=(1 + 1) y=(2 + 2) z=(3 + 3)) hold=(y z) (hold-y x=x y=y z=z))
# => (hold-y x=2 y=(2 + 2) z=6)

(let ((a=1 b=2) (c=(a + b))) hold=c (hold c))   # => (' (1 + 2))

A bind=(x y) option names bindings that are bound, not substituted: each
value is evaluated and installed as a lexical name instead of being written into
the body. Bound and substituted names live side by side, so a substituted value
may mention a bound name and resolves against it. The option goes on the let
form, or on a sequence binding form’s own map (where a :let marker must put it):(let ((const=2.551 f=((a ^ 2) / ((a + b) ^ 2)))
      (a=(2 * const) b=(4 * (const ^ 2))) hold=f bind=(a b))
  f)                                     # => 0.02685688214587777

(do :let ((a=1) (b=(a + 1)) bind=(a b)) (+ a b))   # => 3

const substitutes into a and b; a and b are bound; hold=f inserts
f’s expression, which then evaluates against the bound a and b. A name
cannot be both held and bound. let= already binds every name and takes neither
option.

Because a value is inserted rather than looked up, a value whose head is its own
name is harmless: (let (db=(db 1)) db) is (db 1).

A table is air’s tabular value: named, typed, ordered columns of immutable
data, with an optional unique index. It is a persistent value like a form — an
update returns a new table and leaves the old one untouched — and it is backed
by Air’s persistent vectors and dictionaries, so a column access is O(1), a cell
update is O(log n), and updates share structure with the table they came from.

A table is column-major. (columns t) preserves the declared order, a column
returns as an ordinary sequence, and a row returns as an ordinary map form whose
keys are the column names.(table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42))
# => #table(2×2: age, name)

Tables are an immutable extern type (AirTable), not a form: a schema and type
information cannot live in a plain form, and a plain sequence of row maps would
make a column access O(n) and a cell update O(n). Everything below is an
ordinary air value operation on top of that representation.

There are two spellings, and they build the same table:(table (name="Bob" age=51) (name="Sue" age=42))   # sequence elements are rows
(table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42))            # map entries are columns
(eq? (table (name="Bob" age=51) (name="Sue" age=42))
     (table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42)))      # => true

Rows. Each sequence element is a map-only form; every row must name the
same columns, or the constructor raises.

Columns. Each map value is a sequence (its cells), naught (an empty
column), or a scalar (a one-element column). Every column must have the same
length.

Rows and columns may not be mixed in one call.

The reserved keys columns=, types=, na=, and index= configure the table
rather than naming a column. A column literally named one of them is written
with row syntax or with (table columns=(…) …). With no rows or columns,
columns= names the columns and gives a typed 0-row table.(table)                                    # => #table(0×0)
(table columns=(:a :b) types=(a=:int))     # => #table(0×2: a, b)
(table b=(1) a=(2) columns=(:b :a))        # the order is b, a

Without columns=, the names are sorted by their text, so (table b=(1) a=(2))
prints #table(1×2: a, b). The order matters only for display and output; it
does not affect equality.

A cell is plain immutable air data: a scalar, a string, a keyword or symbol, or
a nested plain container. An extern (including bytes and another table), a
mutable, or a reference form is refused.

Each column records a type and an NA marker in its metadata. The types
are :int, :float, :number, :string, :bool, :symbol, :keyword,
:naught, and :any. The type is inferred from the non-missing cells unless
types= overrides it:(schema (table a=(1 2) b=(1 2.5) c=(true false) d=("x" "y")))
# => (a=(na=NA type=:int) b=(na=NaN type=:number)
#     c=(na=NA type=:bool) d=(na=NA type=:string))

A column with one cell type is that type; mixed integers and floats are
:number; a mix across families is :any; an all-missing column is :naught.
types= coerces, so strings can be parsed into numbers:(get (table a=("1" "2") types=(a=:int)) :a)    # => (1 2)

Missing data is in band. A cell equal to its column’s NA marker is missing;
there is no separate null. Each column’s default marker is NaN for a
:float/:number column and the predefined symbol NA for every other column,
and na= declares a different marker:(schema (table a=(1 2)))            # => (a=(na=NA type=:int))
(schema (table a=(1.0 2.0)))        # => (a=(na=NaN type=:float))
(schema (table a=(1 0) na=(a=0)))   # => (a=(na=0 type=:int))
(get (table a=(1 0) na=(a=0)) :a)   # => (1 0), and 0 is missing

An explicit marker is authoritative: with na=(a=0) the canonical NA and
NaN are ordinary data and are type-checked. The cost of an in-band marker is
that a legitimate value equal to the marker is indistinguishable from missing;
declare a different na= where that matters. In particular, a real NaN in a
float column is missing unless the column declares another marker.

NA is a fixed point of reduction: NA reduces to itself and no binding or
definition may shadow it ((let (NA=5) NA) raises). It is distinct from the
keyword :NA and the string "NA".

get is the single accessor. An integer names a row, a keyword (or a string
naming a column) names a column, and any other key is looked up in the index.(let (t=(table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42)))
  ((get t :age)          # the whole column: => (51 42)
   (get t 1)             # a row map: => (age=51 name="Bob")
   (get t 1 :age)        # a cell: => 51
   (get t :age 1)))      # the same cell in the other order: => 51

Row 0 is the table itself, negative rows count from the end, and default=
supplies a value when the row or column is missing. nth, first, last,
second, third, and rest treat the table as its rows; count and length
are the row count. A table is not a sequence: join, merge, and update-in
refuse it rather than silently downgrading it.

Every update returns a new table.(with t :age (60 70))        # replace a whole column (or add one)
(with t 2 (age=99))          # update the named cells of a row
(with t 2 (age=99))          # a partial row leaves the other columns alone
(with t (2 :age) 99)         # set one cell — row then column
(with t score=(1 2))         # a map entry also names a column

: is the wildcard for “all rows” or “all columns”, so (with t (: :age) v)
is (with t :age v) and (with t (2 :) v) is (with t 2 v); a lone : names
neither and raises (the wildcard’s meaning on ordinary forms — every entry of
the level — is in 

the data model).
A new column’s type and NA are inferred from its values,
an existing column’s metadata is enforced, and a value of the wrong type or
length raises. A table cell is always a value, so a table reduces its update
value before inserting it.(push t (name="Z" age=3))    # a positional map appends a row
(push t score=(1 2))         # a map entry appends a column
(pop t)                      # remove the last row
(drop t 2)                   # remove a row
(wout t :age)                # remove a column
(wout t (2 :age))            # set one cell to its column's NA

A table is an ordinary form container for the hold- family. hold-get returns
a column, row, or cell held; hold-with, hold-push, and hold-wout return the
updated table held; and an inserted held value contributes its content, because a
table cell is always a value. hold=false asks for the plain result, and a
held table is opaque to the hold-blind accessors, so read from one with
hold-get:(hold-get t :age)                                # => (' 51 42)
(hold-get (hold-with t :age (' (60 70))) :age)   # => (' 60 70)
(hold-get (hold-push t score=(' (3 4))) :score)  # => (' 3 4)

A column may be declared the table’s index with index=:name. Every value
in it must be a scalar, non-missing, and unique; those values then address rows:(let (t=(table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42) index=:name))
  ((get t "Bob")                        # => (age=51 name="Bob")
   (get (with t ("Bob" :age) 60) "Bob")))   # => (age=60 name="Bob")

(table-index t) is the index column, or naught. Integer keys always mean
row positions, so an index column whose values are integers is not addressable
by a bare integer key. Every update maintains the index: a cell or row change
replaces the old key, push inserts, pop and row removal delete, and removing
the index column clears the declaration. Duplicate or missing index values
raise.

The collection verbs treat a table as its rows, building one row map at a time:(let (t=(table name=("Bob" "Sue") age=(51 42)))
  ((for (r t) r.age)                        # => (51 42)
   (map (?r -> r.age) t)                    # => (51 42)
   (filter (?r -> (r.age > 45)) t)          # => ((age=51 name="Bob"))
   (reduce ((?a ?r) -> (a + r.age)) 0 t)))  # => 93

map with depth=0 maps the table itself. haskey and in test a row or a
column, and a 0-row table iterates zero times, so reduce returns its initial
accumulator.

eq? compares tables by content: the same rows and cells, the same column
metadata (type and NA), and the same index declaration. Column order is not
part of equality, matching air’s map semantics; columns still preserves it
for output. hash follows eq?.

Printing is a summary, never the cells: #table(2×2: age, name) and, with an
index, #table(2×2: age, name; index=name).

A table is stored in its namespace’s database like any value, using its
serialization registration. Like every unnamed extern, it survives a database
write in the same process but cannot be reconstructed from to-json/from-json
text, which yields a dead extern. Do not use the serialization JSON as a
transport; use encode/decode with a data format instead.

decode with format=:csv or :tsv returns a table, and encode accepts a
table or a non-empty sequence of row maps. The format options — header,
column-delimiter, row-delimiter, types, na, columns, and index — are
described in 

Data formats.(decode "name,age\nBob,51\nSue,42" format=:csv)     # => #table(2×2: name, age)
(encode (table a=(1 2) b=("x" "y")) format=:csv)    # => "a,b\n1,x\n2,y\n"

Missing data is in band: a real value equal to the NA marker cannot be
distinguished from missing.

An integer-valued index column is not addressable by a bare key, because an
integer always names a row position.

A table’s cells are plain data, so a table cannot hold an extern, a mutable, or
a reference form.

Saving a table as a SQL table is a planned follow-up; the extern is already
persistent, but it is not mapped onto columns and rows in the database.

(check expr) evaluates expr and returns a boolean. Inside a (test name body…) it also records the outcome: a falsy expression is a failure, and an
uncaught error in the body is recorded as one failure and ends the body. The
name is evaluated, so it may be a string, keyword, or any other value. The
result is a data form (name=<name> pass=<n> fail=<n> failures=(<failure>…)),
where each failure is the held failing expression (or the caught error form), so
evaluating the summary again does not run it:(test "addition" (check (== (+ 1 2) 3)) (check (== (* 2 3) 7)))
# => (fail=1 failures=((' == (* 2 3) 7)) name="addition" pass=1)

A check may sit anywhere in the body — inside a helper def, a doseq, or a
branch — because it records into whichever test is running. A plain truth test
(true?) or a bare expression records nothing, so a failing check inside a
helper would otherwise pass vacuously.

Counters are task-local, so tests running on separate tasks do not interfere,
and a nested test reports only its own body.

Air has no separate time type. A time is the ordinary immutable form(time 1761686100.123)

whose single element is a floating-point count of seconds since the Unix epoch,
in UTC. Because it is an ordinary form it persists, serializes, hashes, and
compares like any other value; the printer, the arithmetic operators, and the
verbs below are the only things that know it is a moment rather than a call.

Times print as ISO-8601 in UTC:(now)                     # => (time "2026-10-29T06:43:02.663Z")
(time "2026-10-28")       # => (time "2026-10-28T00:00:00Z")

A value with finer than millisecond precision (or outside the range a
DateTime can represent) keeps its numeric spelling instead —
(time 1.0e-7) — so a printed time always reads back as exactly the same
value.

(now) is the current instant. It is a pure value: it needs no database and is
unaffected by a transaction. (time? x) tests the type.

(time x) converts x to a time: a number is UTC epoch seconds, a time is
itself, and an ISO-8601 string is parsed. Anything else is left symbolic, like
every other math verb.

Accepted strings include a date alone, a date and time, a space or T
separator, a fractional second, and a Z or ±hh:mm/±hhmm offset:(time "2026-10-28")                    # midnight UTC
(time "2026-10-28T21:15")              # midnight seconds
(time "2026-10-28 21:15:00.123")       # a fractional second
(time "2026-10-28T21:15:00.123+02:00") # the same instant, in UTC

A string that is not a valid time raises a catchable error rather than staying
symbolic, since it was meant as a time.

(time-str t) is the inverse: ISO-8601 UTC with milliseconds, trailing zeros
trimmed. Two options refine it:(time-str (now))                                   # "2026-10-29T06:43:02.663Z"
(time-str (now) format="yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS")      # "2026-10-29 06:43:02"
(time-str (now) offset="+02:00")                   # "2026-10-29T08:43:02.663+02:00"

format is a Julia 

Dates
DateFormat string, whose tokens are not strftime’s: lowercase m is the
month, d the day, and H the hour, but MM is minutes, SS seconds, and
lowercase s milliseconds. So the strftime format %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S is
written yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS — not yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:ss, which would print
milliseconds where the seconds belong. offset= shifts the instant before
formatting and replaces the Z; a number of seconds works too.

DateTime carries milliseconds, so formatting and the printed ISO spelling are
millisecond-exact; the underlying Float64 keeps the full precision for
arithmetic.

A time behaves like a real number of seconds in the operations where that
reading makes sense:(+ (now) 60)              # one minute from now  (a time)
(+ 60 (now))              # the same
(- (now) (now))           # a duration in seconds (a number)
(- (now) 3600)            # an hour ago (a time)

A time minus a time is a number of seconds; a time plus or minus a number is a
time. Everything else — time + time, time × number, unary minus on a time —
stays symbolic, so a form you did not mean to reduce is left alone.

Ordering works on two times:(< (time 1) (time 2))                  # => true

A time and a plain number do not compare: < stays symbolic rather than
guessing that the number is epoch seconds. Use the explicit verbs when a value
might be either:

verb

meaning

(before? a b)

a is earlier than b

(after? a b)

a is later than b

(between? x lo hi)

lo ≤ x ≤ hi, inclusive

All three accept times and numbers (a time contributes its seconds), and a
symbolic argument leaves the form unchanged.(between? (now) (- (now) 1) (+ (now) 1))   # => true
(between? 1 0 2)                            # => true

The printer spells a time as (time "…Z") both flat and in the


pretty printer, so layout decisions measure the same text. The
JSON codec knows nothing about times: a time is an ordinary form and encodes
structurally, with no database resource.(to-json (time 0.5))     # => "[[\":time\", 0.5], {}]"

lib/time/init.air adds readable spellings for durations and instants:(using time (minutes 90))      # => 5400
(using time (hours 2))         # => 7200
(using time (days 1))          # => 86400
(using time (weeks 1))         # => 604800

(seconds n) is n itself; the rest are multiples. Two helpers read better
than arithmetic in prose:(since t)          # seconds elapsed between t and now
(ago (hours 1))    # the instant one hour ago(using time (between? (ago (days 1)) (- (now) (days 2)) (now)))

The library loads lazily the first time it is referenced, as
.lib.time (see 

Loading files and libraries).

Air has an abstract user interface. A UI is a tree of ordinary air forms headed
ui; the forms describe what an element means, not how it is drawn, so the
same tree can be presented by a terminal over SSH, by a web page, or by any
other renderer that follows the contract. Air owns the values, the validation,
the callbacks, and the facts an element asserts; a renderer is only a view.(ui-open :prefs
  (ui column
    (ui label text="Experiment configuration")
    (ui text-input id=:experiment-name initval="experiment-01"
                   label="Experiment name" assert=(experiment-name _))
    (ui dropdown id=:device options=(("CPU" :cpu) ("GPU" :gpu))
                 initval=:gpu label="Compute device" assert=(compute-device _))
    (ui slider id=:threshold initval=0.8 min=0.0 max=1.0 step=0.01
               label="Confidence threshold" assert=(confidence-threshold _))
    (ui button label="Done" on-click=(() -> (ui-dismiss! :prefs)))))
(ui-show :prefs)
(ui-values :prefs)          ; => (device=:gpu experiment-name="experiment-01" …)
(facts .main)               ; => (' (compute-device :gpu) …)

The forms resemble widgets in the style of ipywidgets, but an element’s value
lives in the UI runtime, not in a renderer, and an assert makes that value an
ordinary fact that rules and functions use without knowing a UI exists.

Interface independence. A (ui …) form names a semantic element, not a
terminal or web control.

Composability. Elements nest arbitrarily; layout elements arrange other
elements.

Statefulness. Interactive elements hold a value air can read and update.

Reactivity. A change can run a callback and revise a fact.

Validation. Air validates every value itself; a renderer may help, but
it is never trusted.

Identity. An element may carry an id that survives a redraw or an
update.

Extensibility. New widget kinds follow the same conventions; a renderer
that cannot present one must say so rather than substitute different
semantics.

hierarchy.lvl2: A UI tree is inert data
A UI tree is inert data

records.content:
ui is a reserved head, like error and signal: a form headed ui never
reduces, at any depth, so a tree is descriptive data until ui-open
instantiates it.(ui checkbox initval=true)                    ; => (ui checkbox initval=true)
(ui label text=(+ 1 2))                       ; => (ui label text=(+ 1 2))

That is what keeps assert= and on-change= raw: (ui …) is data, and the
runtime evaluates the parameters it understands itself, at instantiation.
let and with still build trees, because they substitute textually before
evaluating:(let (n=0.8)
  (ui slider initval=n min=0.0 max=1.0 label="Threshold"))

Every parameter except assert is evaluated once when ui-open instantiates
the element, so a parameter may be any expression —
initval=(get $.config.threshold) just works. assert is evaluated with _
bound to the element’s current value, there and on every change.

parameter

meaning

id

a keyword, symbol, or string naming the element within its instance

label

human-readable text; descriptive, never an identifier

description

supplementary explanatory text

disabled

a Boolean; a disabled element still displays its value but a user may not change it

An id is unique within an instance (a duplicate is an error) and independent
of position in the tree. (ui-values :k) and (ui-set! :k :id v) address
elements by it. An element without an id is still a distinct element with an
internal path; it can carry assert=/on-change= but air cannot address it.
Other forms of id are rejected with a clear error.

A disabled element refuses a user change — the renderer reports it as
invalid — while air itself may still update it with ui-set!.

An interactive element holds a current value. initval establishes it; a kind
with a type-specific default (false for checkbox, "" for text-input, …)
may omit it. Two parameters let a change participate in the rest of air.

A function called after a value change has been accepted and installed:(ui checkbox id=:debug initval=false label="Enable debugging"
  on-change=((?old ?new) -> (record-change old new)))

It is not called at creation (initialization is not a change), and it is not
called when an update does not actually change the value. An error it raises
propagates as an ordinary air error; the value stays installed.

A fact form evaluated with _ bound to the element’s current value:(ui checkbox initval=false label="Enable debugging"
  assert=(if _ (debugging-enabled true) naught))

The result must be a fact or naught. When the element is instantiated the
fact is asserted; on every change the element’s assertion is revised to the
new result, in one logical revision, so the old fact never coexists with its
replacement. naught retracts it, and an identical result is a no-op. Either
on-change or assert may be supplied without the other.

The assertion is maintained in the namespace that was current when the
element was instantiated, even if the process later switches namespaces, and
it therefore needs writefact there. The runtime labels every fact it asserts
with a reason unique to the instance and element, so retracting our fact never
disturbs an identical fact asserted elsewhere by other air code:(assert (experiment-name "xyz"))   ; asserted independently
(ui-set! :a :n "other")            ; our labeled record is revised
(facts .main)                      ; (experiment-name "xyz") survives

Removing an element — by ui-update! or ui-close! — retracts only the fact
that element owned.

Air validates every incoming value before accepting it; a renderer never
validates.

The value, the constraint, and the error message are air’s.

An invalid update changes nothing: no value, no callback, no assertion
revision.

A renderer is told the reason and displays it, keeping the last accepted
value.

(ui-set! :k :id v) raises (error :ui-invalid :id "reason") for the same
failure.

The constraints are per kind: bounds, step alignment, option membership,
lo ≤ hi, non-empty required text, and so on. See the catalog below.

checkbox and toggle hold true or false; the difference is
presentational. initval defaults to false.(ui checkbox initval=true label="Dark Mode?")
(ui toggle initval=false label="Enable debugging")

text-input and text-area hold a string; text-area also takes rows=.
password-input holds a string too, but the renderer obscures it — visual
obscuring is not secure storage: the value is an ordinary air value,
reachable by ui-values and by assert.

initval defaults to "", placeholder is an optional hint, and
required=true rejects an empty string.(ui text-input initval="" label="Search" placeholder="Enter search terms...")
(ui text-area initval="" label="Notes" rows=8)
(ui password-input label="API Token" placeholder="Enter token...")

int-input holds an integer, float-input a number; both take optional min,
max, and step (default 1). slider is a bounded number and requires
min and max; it also takes orientation= (:horizontal or :vertical),
readout= (show the value), and continuous-update= (communicate while
dragging rather than on release). These four require initval — unlike a
Boolean or a string, an uninitialized number has no sensible default.(ui int-input initval=1000 min=1 max=100000 label="Number of iterations")

keyword, symbol, or string; the colon is dropped, so :prefs and "prefs" name
the same instance.

ui-open returns the key as a keyword; with no key it generates one (:ui1,
:ui2, …). A key already in use is an error. Instances are owned by the user
who opened them: air sees them all, another user sees only its own, and an
operation on someone else’s instance raises an error.

ui-update! re-instantiates the tree in one step. An element whose id
survives keeps its current value when the new kind still accepts it (so a
surviving field is not reset to its new initval), new elements take their
initval, removed elements’ facts are retracted, and changed parameters take
effect.

ui-close! is idempotent, so a cleanup path need not know whether the UI
already closed itself.

A renderer is a view over an instance. It reads the tree, values, and
validation reasons, presents them somehow, and reports only semantic events —
(:set id value), (:click id), (:dismiss) — which the runtime routes
through one validated update path. It never validates, stores, or asserts
anything, and it never echoes an engine-originated update back, because it has
no path to do so.

The runtime notifies every attached renderer after every accepted change,
including a programmatic one, so multiple views of one instance stay in step.
An equal-value set is a no-op, so a redraw loop cannot oscillate.

(ui-render :k width=80) is the headless renderer, for documentation and tests.
It is deterministic: a column stacks, a row shares a line, a group
indents, tabs shows the first tab, and a checkbox is [x] or [ ].(ui-open :r (ui column
  (ui label text="Config")
  (ui text-input id=:n initval="exp-01" label="Name")
  (ui dropdown id=:d options=(("CPU" :cpu) ("GPU" :gpu)) initval=:gpu
               label="Device")))
(ui-render :r)      ; => "Config\nName: exp-01\nDevice: GPU"

(ui-show :k) requires an interactive SSH session (src/ssh/); otherwise it
raises (error :no-renderer …). It enters the alternate screen, draws a frame,
redraws in place (clearing one line at a time rather than the whole screen, to
avoid flicker), and restores the screen and cursor in finally.

Focus is the renderer’s, and Tab / Shift-Tab (or Up / Down) cycle through the
value-bearing and button elements:

Space toggles a checkbox or toggle, activates a button, or begins editing
a text field with a space;

Enter activates a button or commits a text field edit;

Left/Right step numbers, sliders, and selection widgets; Home/End jump to
the bounds or the first/last option; in a multi-select, Left/Right moves the
selection and Space toggles it;

printable characters edit a text element with a drawn cursor.

A text or slider edit commits on Enter or when focus leaves the element; there
is no key release in a terminal, so that is what continuous-update=false
means.

There are two ways out, deliberately different:

Esc dismisses gracefully: the screen is restored and ui-show returns
naught.

Ctrl-C aborts: the screen is restored and ui-show raises
(error :ctrl-c), exactly as Ctrl-C at the REPL prompt raises :ctrl-c, so a
surrounding except (or the REPL) handles it like any other error.

A Done button that calls (ui-dismiss! :k) is the same graceful path.
Validation failures appear on the status line, and the display keeps the last
accepted value.

Creation. ui-open reduces the tree once and instantiates each element:
the kind is checked, every parameter is evaluated in the caller’s scope, and
an assert/on-change keeps the lexical names it will need when it fires.

Initialization. Defaults and initval establish values; initial
assertions are evaluated and asserted. A failure here retracts whatever was
already asserted and leaves no instance behind.

Presentation. One or more renderers display the instance.

Interaction. A renderer reports a semantic event.

Revision. Air validates and accepts or rejects it, installs the value,
revises the assertion, and runs the callback.

Removal. ui-update! or ui-close! retracts the facts the removed
elements owned, never facts asserted elsewhere.

A callbacks and assertions run in the namespace, val bindings, and identity
captured at instantiation, so a UI opened inside (namespace .app …) keeps
writing .app even when the value is changed from another namespace or task.

Afterwards the selections are ordinary facts, so a rule can use
(compute-device ?d) without knowing where ?d came from.

A shown UI is modal. ui-show owns the session until it is dismissed;
there is no non-blocking dashboard yet.

The terminal renderer needs a pty. A local stty-driven renderer, a web
renderer, and incremental subtree updates are follow-ups; the abstract layer
and the text renderer are the contract they must meet.

Passwords are obscured, not protected. A password-input value is an
ordinary form, readable with ui-values and assertable like any other.
